passages: The article " Meta Platforms Unveils Muse AI Agent, Expands Smart Glasses and VR Push " was originally published by MarketBeat.
Meta unveiled Muse , a personal AI agent designed to manage tasks, information and interactions across devices.
It is expanding in Canada and will connect with services such as Spotify, Shopify, PayPal and Instacart, with Meta planning to monetize transactions over time.

Meta is upgrading its smart glasses with ongoing Muse voice conversations, background assistance, privacy-focused processing and features including live translation and FDA-cleared hearing enhancement.
The company also introduced new audio-glasses designs and expanded Ray-Ban Meta styles.
Meta announced Meta VR Glasses , a roughly 100-gram immersive device for entertainment, gaming and multi-monitor computing, scheduled to ship in spring at $1,299.

The keynote speaker said Meta plans in the coming weeks to upgrade the AI experience on Meta Glasses, enabling users to hold ongoing voice conversations with their Muse rather than receive only a single response to a request.
The company was founded as Facebook in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg and was renamed Meta Platforms in 2021 to reflect its broader focus on building the metaverse.
He added that Meta opened its Connector Platform to developers the prior week and had received more than 1,500 applications.
Muse, which Meta said it shipped several weeks ago, is intended to evolve into a personal agent used by billions of people.
The company said each Muse has its own private and secure virtual machine, or Muse secure VM, and that the Muse Spark model is trained specifically for personal-agent tasks.
Meta also announced Computer Vision capabilities for Muse on Mac.
It is also building private processing for glasses, which it said will allow certain AI features to run in a secure server environment where neither Meta nor others can access users' data.
Meta Platforms, Inc develops technologies that help people connect, communicate and build communities online.
Meta said its Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, which include full-color displays and the Meta Neural Band, will become available online through meta.com and begin an international rollout.
Meta said Disney+, Peacock, Paramount+, HBO Max, YouTube, Prime Video and Crunchyroll will offer content on the platform.

Meta recently launched a Muse Mac app that can work across users' files, messages, calendars and notes, according to Wang.
The company highlighted an expanding network of connectors that link Muse to external services.
Meta said Muse will be free for a large number of tokens, with the company expecting over time to profit by taking a small fee from transactions.
Finally, Meta previewed Muse Charm, a keychain-sized device designed to provide quick access to the Muse experience through a fingerprint sensor, voice interaction and a camera.

It is also building private processing for glasses, which it said will allow certain AI features to run in a secure server environment where neither Meta nor others can access users' data. Meta said it will begin rolling out the technology for features such as live translation.

Users will be able to take a guided assessment in the companion app and tune amplification to their hearing needs, according to the company.

Meta said its Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, which include full-color displays and the Meta Neural Band, will become available online through meta.com and begin an international rollout. By the end of the year, the company expects to offer more than 100 glasses styles.

Andrew Bosworth, Meta's Chief Technology Officer, said the device is IMAX Enhanced certified and supports Dolby Atmos spatial audio and Dolby Vision. It will support the Quest library with optional controllers, Xbox Cloud Gaming, and 75 hands-only titles at launch, according to Bosworth.

Meta said Disney+, Peacock, Paramount+, HBO Max, YouTube, Prime Video and Crunchyroll will offer content on the platform. The company also said it plans more than 100 immersive sports events per year, including ESPN programming beginning with college football on Quest this fall.
Meta VR Glasses are scheduled to ship in the spring for $1,299.

Finally, Meta previewed Muse Charm, a keychain-sized device designed to provide quick access to the Muse experience through a fingerprint sensor, voice interaction and a camera. The company said it expects Muse Charm to be ready to ship in December and plans to provide additional details later.

sources.title: Meta is working on making Muse its smart glasses assistant - Android Authority
passages: Meta is preparing to make its new AI agent Muse the brains behind its smart glasses, potentially replacing the standard Meta AI with a significantly more autonomous assistant.
A separate leak shared by Wong on X shows Meta is also working on “Meta Pay for Muse,” developing a native wallet interface for Muse with Meta Pay support, alongside Stripe’s Link and Shop Pay.
The integration appears designed to enable the agent to execute real-world transactions and make secure purchases on a user’s behalf.

The leaked setup screen, titled “Enable Impacc as your glasses assistant?” (where “Impacc” likely refers to an internal codename for Muse), notes that Muse is in beta and will allow users to swap back to Meta AI whenever they prefer.

Interestingly, the prompt explicitly lists features that are not yet available in the beta, tipping Meta’s hand on what is coming: Live AI, Navigation, Shazam song identification, Strava, and Health Connect integrations.
The move fits cleanly alongside Meta’s broader hardware roadmap.
The company currently dominates the market for smart-glasses shipments , and recent reports indicate it is exploring camera-free smart glasses focused entirely on ambient voice interactions .
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.

Adding turn-by-turn navigation and fitness-tracking capabilities would transform Meta’s eyewear from a passive conversational accessory into an active, hands-free personal enabler device, just like your phone.
Wearers could perhaps track a run in Strava or ask the glasses to guide them home entirely by voice.

passages: If you're willing to trust it with the most sensitive parts of your digital life, it can use the web, book travel, make phone calls, send emails and even make purchases on your behalf.
So far, you can use Muse in its standalone iOS, Android or Mac apps, or within your WhatsApp chats.
But in "the coming months," Meta is bringing its errand-running agent to its AI glasses.
But that gets to a question about how much Muse for glasses really adds: agentic AI's appeal is that it does things in the background without constant supervision.
Pulling out your phone to give it a new task doesn't exactly sound like much of a burden.
The glasses do make that hands-free, and Meta suggested some situations where that could be useful: guiding personalized workouts, logging meals and providing nutritional insights.
But that sounds like more of a convenience than a necessity.
Meta shared more details about Muse for AI glasses at its Connect 2026 event on Wednesday.

The company said Muse will help you "stay on top of things, take tasks and projects off your plate and turn long-term goals into action plans, all hands-free." Specific examples include booking appointments, checking flight prices and tracking down items.

Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. It is expanding in Canada and will connect with services such as Spotify, Shopify, PayPal and Instacart, with Meta planning to monetize transactions over time.

Meta is upgrading its smart glasses with ongoing Muse voice conversations, background assistance, privacy-focused processing and features including live translation and FDA-cleared hearing enhancement.
The company also introduced new audio-glasses designs and expanded Ray-Ban Meta styles.
Meta announced Meta VR Glasses , a roughly 100-gram immersive device for entertainment, gaming and multi-monitor computing, scheduled to ship in spring at $1,299.

The keynote speaker said Meta plans in the coming weeks to upgrade the AI experience on Meta Glasses, enabling users to hold ongoing voice conversations with their Muse rather than receive only a single response to a request.
The company was founded as Facebook in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg and was renamed Meta Platforms in 2021 to reflect its broader focus on building the metaverse.
He added that Meta opened its Connector Platform to developers the prior week and had received more than 1,500 applications.
Muse, which Meta said it shipped several weeks ago, is intended to evolve into a personal agent used by billions of people.
The company said each Muse has its own private and secure virtual machine, or Muse secure VM, and that the Muse Spark model is trained specifically for personal-agent tasks.
Meta also announced Computer Vision capabilities for Muse on Mac.
It is also building private processing for glasses, which it said will allow certain AI features to run in a secure server environment where neither Meta nor others can access users' data.

The leaked setup screen, titled “Enable Impacc as your glasses assistant?” (where “Impacc” likely refers to an internal codename for Muse), notes that Muse is in beta and will allow users to swap back to Meta AI whenever they prefer.

The move fits cleanly alongside Meta’s broader hardware roadmap.
The company currently dominates the market for smart-glasses shipments , and recent reports indicate it is exploring camera-free smart glasses focused entirely on ambient voice interactions .

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date. CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. passages: YouTube Music is rolling out some fun new features, including the expansion of the "hum to search" tool that has been in beta for Android users since March.
It's also been working on something called AI-generated conversational radio.
This isn't a platform in which AI DJs take jobs away from Wolfman Jack or whatever.
Rather, it's a tool that lets people use natural conversation to describe the type of radio station they want to listen to.
The algorithm will take in that information and create some tailor-made radio.
This is sort of like Spotify's AI DJ from a while back , but the conversational element should make the algorithm zero in on your exact tastes as described.

sources.title: YouTube Music is testing its answer to Spotify AI DJ– and early users can’t decide it they love it or hate it - TechRadar
passages: YouTube Music's answer to Spotify's AI DJ is far from perfect and is still a beta experiment.
But with a few tweaks here and there it could surface as one of the music streamer's best features.
Based on the early reactions from test users, there’s hope for the service’s venture into AI-based experiences – as long as YouTube listens to that user feedback.
Instead, some have credited it for its natural interjections and unintrusive commentary.
The voices themselves have also been praised, but more seem to be in favor of the female host rather than the male host.

When Spotify rolled out AI DJ in 2023, it sparked a huge debate about AI’s presence within music streaming, but was also criticized – especially for its lack of new music recommendations and jarring voiceover.
I was one of those critics, but warmed up to it when Spotify introduced its song requests feature .
It’s still in its infancy, but users are already gathering their thoughts.
Though YouTube Music’s new feature has largely gone down well, it isn't the biggest feature that users have been asking for.
Others simply hate the concept in general, with Reddit user 'ptrckl_' stating "I just wanna listen to my music".

YouTube Music is lagging behind other music streaming services when it comes to features like Spotify's AI DJ, but it's just started rolling out its own radio-style trick to beta testers as part of its YouTube Labs initiative . At the moment YouTube Labs is only accessible to a limited number of Premium beta testers in the US, and we don’t know when this program will be available in other markets. However, more users are starting to get their hands on YouTube Music’s AI host – and despite the disregard for AI music streaming features in general, the reactions have been pretty positive. When Spotify rolled out AI DJ in 2023, it sparked a huge debate about AI’s presence within music streaming, but was also criticized – especially for its lack of new music recommendations and jarring voiceover. I was one of those critics, but warmed up to it when Spotify introduced its song requests feature . As for YouTube Music, it’s a two-voice host rather than a DJ, but has a similar effect. Rather than existing as a separate entity in the YouTube Music app, the AI DJ icon appears next to the 'thumbs up / down' buttons in the playback screen when you’re listening to radio and mixes. It’s still in its infancy, but users are already gathering their thoughts. The main difference between YouTube Music’s AI host and Spotify’s AI DJ is that it offers "relevant stories, fan trivia, and fun commentary" in your listening session, while Spotify’s AI DJ simply introduces the next segment of songs. Rather than segueing from one song to the next, YouTube Music’s AI host injects music trivia into the voiceover – which is going down well with music nerds. The most common frustration is its failed attempts at cheesy humor and there are also seemingly some factual inaccuracies (which YouTube has addressed). Others simply hate the concept in general, with Reddit user 'ptrckl_' stating "I just wanna listen to my music". But overall, most testers have expressed their appreciation for the addition of music facts weaved into their streaming experience. Where users complained about Spotify AI DJ being invasive, the opposite is being said about YouTube Music’s AI host. Instead, some have credited it for its natural interjections and unintrusive commentary. The voices themselves have also been praised, but more seem to be in favor of the female host rather than the male host. Though YouTube Music’s new feature has largely gone down well, it isn't the biggest feature that users have been asking for. In addition to other basic functions such as searching within playlists and volume normalization, some have noted that YouTube has yet to introduce a ‘liked songs’ library, a simple feature on other major platforms. Not only is YouTube Music seemingly ignoring the small requests from users, it appears that its AI DJ competitor cannot be disabled permanently – at least for now. Still, in between these common frustrations there's a surprising wave of support for YouTube Music’s AI host, particularly its commentary, so hopefully a refined version will ultimately get a wider rollout. coreStoryFacts.text: YouTube Music is rolling out some fun new features, including the expansion of the "hum to search" tool that has been in beta for Android users since March.
It's also been working on something called AI-generated conversational radio.
This isn't a platform in which AI DJs take jobs away from Wolfman Jack or whatever.
Rather, it's a tool that lets people use natural conversation to describe the type of radio station they want to listen to.
The algorithm will take in that information and create some tailor-made radio.
This is sort of like Spotify's AI DJ from a while back , but the conversational element should make the algorithm zero in on your exact tastes as described.
YouTube Music today is making official sound search, while acknowledging that it’s testing the “AI-generated conversational radio” for US Premium subscribers.
It lets you create a custom radio by “describing exactly what they want to hear.”
It simply lets you query YTM’s “catalog of over 100 million official songs by sound.” Some users had it in May before the feature was rolled back for whatever reason.

Once available, you can tap the magnifying glass icon in the top-right corner of YouTube Music to access a waveform button. (It appears next to the existing microphone for voice search.) This launches a fullscreen UI that lets you sing, hum, or play a song.

Based on the early reactions from test users, there’s hope for the service’s venture into AI-based experiences – as long as YouTube listens to that user feedback.
Instead, some have credited it for its natural interjections and unintrusive commentary.
The voices themselves have also been praised, but more seem to be in favor of the female host rather than the male host.

It’s still in its infancy, but users are already gathering their thoughts.

YouTube Music is lagging behind other music streaming services when it comes to features like Spotify's AI DJ, but it's just started rolling out its own radio-style trick to beta testers as part of its YouTube Labs initiative . sources.title: YouTube Music gets more conversational with new AI features
passages: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.
Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists.
The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets.
Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.
The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services.
YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.
Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener.
It can then move directly into suggested episodes.

extraction.body: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss. Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. extraction.body: "No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent," the talent agency said in a statement Wednesday night. Meta , led by CEO and AI enthusiast Mark Zuckerberg, this week rolled out the first photo and video tools to come out of its Superintelligence Labs: Muse Photo and Muse Video. The tool brings Meta in line with the state of the art in AI media creation, alongside Google’s Gemini and Seedance 2.0, but along with the tools, Meta also said that all public Instagram profiles will be opt-out, not opt-in, and other users can pull in those other accounts that don’t opt out and create new content using their profiles. For celebrities and other high-profile figures, that could be a major problem, even if most do end up opting out. Now Creative Artists Agency is calling out Meta for the move, and asking the tech giant to make it opt-in, not opt-out. “No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent. True innovation puts creators first: respecting their rights, protecting their livelihoods, and giving them real control, not handing it over to platforms,” CAA said in a statement Wednesday evening. “We have raised our concerns with Meta on behalf of our clients, voicing our disapproval and perspective on the need for a more responsible approach. We call on Meta to make protection the default on Muse Image, not the exception, and enable individuals to opt-in if they want to allow usage of their image or likeness for AI content creation. “Artists deserve to decide if and how their likeness and work is used, with consent and the ability to set their own terms,” the statement continues. “This means letting creators impose restrictions, monitor usage, and prevent unauthorized endorsements or exploitation. Responsible AI requires clear disclosures and swift removal of unauthorized content. There must be easy ways to spot, track, and take down misuse, and it should be clear when something is AI-generated. CAA believes in the power of new technology, but not at the cost of individuals’ rights or livelihoods. The future of creativity depends on respecting the ownership and autonomy of those who make it possible.” CAA, of course, is well aware of the opportunities and threats posed by generative AI to its clients. The agency maintains what it calls the “CAA Vault,” where the digital likenesses of its clients reside for potential future monetization and protection, and the agency was the first test user of YouTube’s deepfake detection tool, which rolled out to all of Hollywood earlier this year. The Muse situation is reminiscent of the botches launch of OpenAI’s Sora, which was overrun with well-known IP and the likenesses of many high-profile figures, forcing the AI giant to pivot to an opt-in model, before it scrapped the video model altogether earlier this year. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.

Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date. CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.” Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop. “You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.” Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf. Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping. Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal. The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion. Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks.

Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent.

While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me.

extraction.body: There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta , led by CEO and AI enthusiast Mark Zuckerberg, this week rolled out the first photo and video tools to come out of its Superintelligence Labs: Muse Photo and Muse Video.

The tool brings Meta in line with the state of the art in AI media creation, alongside Google’s Gemini and Seedance 2.0, but along with the tools, Meta also said that all public Instagram profiles will be opt-out, not opt-in, and other users can pull in those other accounts that don’t opt out and create new content using their profiles.
We call on Meta to make protection the default on Muse Image, not the exception, and enable individuals to opt-in if they want to allow usage of their image or likeness for AI content creation.
Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”
Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks.

extraction.body: "No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent," the talent agency said in a statement Wednesday night. Meta , led by CEO and AI enthusiast Mark Zuckerberg, this week rolled out the first photo and video tools to come out of its Superintelligence Labs: Muse Photo and Muse Video. The tool brings Meta in line with the state of the art in AI media creation, alongside Google’s Gemini and Seedance 2.0, but along with the tools, Meta also said that all public Instagram profiles will be opt-out, not opt-in, and other users can pull in those other accounts that don’t opt out and create new content using their profiles. For celebrities and other high-profile figures, that could be a major problem, even if most do end up opting out. Now Creative Artists Agency is calling out Meta for the move, and asking the tech giant to make it opt-in, not opt-out. “No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent. True innovation puts creators first: respecting their rights, protecting their livelihoods, and giving them real control, not handing it over to platforms,” CAA said in a statement Wednesday evening. “We have raised our concerns with Meta on behalf of our clients, voicing our disapproval and perspective on the need for a more responsible approach. We call on Meta to make protection the default on Muse Image, not the exception, and enable individuals to opt-in if they want to allow usage of their image or likeness for AI content creation. “Artists deserve to decide if and how their likeness and work is used, with consent and the ability to set their own terms,” the statement continues. “This means letting creators impose restrictions, monitor usage, and prevent unauthorized endorsements or exploitation. Responsible AI requires clear disclosures and swift removal of unauthorized content. There must be easy ways to spot, track, and take down misuse, and it should be clear when something is AI-generated. CAA believes in the power of new technology, but not at the cost of individuals’ rights or livelihoods. The future of creativity depends on respecting the ownership and autonomy of those who make it possible.” CAA, of course, is well aware of the opportunities and threats posed by generative AI to its clients. The agency maintains what it calls the “CAA Vault,” where the digital likenesses of its clients reside for potential future monetization and protection, and the agency was the first test user of YouTube’s deepfake detection tool, which rolled out to all of Hollywood earlier this year. The Muse situation is reminiscent of the botches launch of OpenAI’s Sora, which was overrun with well-known IP and the likenesses of many high-profile figures, forcing the AI giant to pivot to an opt-in model, before it scrapped the video model altogether earlier this year. After Sora launched, WME said that it was opting out on behalf of all of its clients, the first domino to fall in that model’s short life. “There is a strong need for real protections for artists and creatives as they encounter AI models using their intellectual property, as well as their name, image and likeness,” WME’s digital chief Chris Jacquemin wrote in a memo at the time. “Our position is that artists should have a choice in how they show up in the world and how their likeness is used and we have notified OpenAI that all WME clients be opted out of the latest Sora AI update, regardless of whether IP rights holders have opted out IP our clients are associated with.” With many celebrities, artists, creators and other high-profile figures on Instagram, an opt-out model may not be good enough, especially when their likeness is their livelihood.

Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.” Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop. “You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.” Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf. extraction.body: There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica.
Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform.
They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3.
The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now.
Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions.

extraction.body: Its popular Meta Ray-Ban glasses are now in their third generation, but two new models steal the show: a powerful, slimmed-down version of Meta's Quest headsets capable of virtual and augmented reality modes, and a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban–branded smart glasses, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform. Meta VR Glasses The next evolution of Meta’s Quest VR headset is something truly different. Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles. They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3. They sit on the nose, right in front of your face like glasses, with no headstrap needed. They look and feel more like the virtual display glasses made by companies like Viture, and what Xreal’s Project Aura seems to be shaping up to be—lightweight mixed-reality lenses that let you access virtual spaces without the burden of a VR headset. There are no included controllers, though the device can connect to Meta’s previous Quest controllers or gamepads like an Xbox controller. Form a fist and flick your thumb up or down to scroll the screen. Small prescription lens inserts can be magnetically clipped inside the lenses. (Meta has not shared how much those will cost.) The software is the same that runs on Meta’s Quest VR devices, so movie and game titles in the Quest ecosystem will work on the VR Glasses. The VR Glasses can also display a virtual keyboard on a surface in front of you, then use the embedded cameras to track specific finger placements. The only immediate downside compared to other VR headsets—at least that I could tell from a brief demo at Meta Connect—is that the VR glasses don’t cover your entire field of vision, so it doesn’t feel as immersive as a traditional VR headset. Meta says the VR Glasses cost $1,300 and will ship in the spring of 2027. Ray-Ban Meta Audio Meta has spent the past few months being absolutely pummeled by controversy about the privacy issues inherent in its camera-enabled smart glasses. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses have all the audio capabilities of a standard pair of Meta’s smart glasses, minus image and video capture. At 43 grams, they’re also lighter than the others. They come in 23 different color and style options, including the retro Ray-Ban Clubmaster frame and a more rectangular Burbank. The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 Meta's flagship line of smart glasses is getting a “Gen 3” upgrade. They have 12-MP cameras, like last year, plus 3K Dolby Atmos–enabled video capture. The glasses will get up to nine hours of battery life, two more than their predecessors. A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica. Earlier this summer, Meta debuted smart glasses under its own branding, which cost a little less but were functionally identical to the Ray-Ban models. Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions. These Meta-branded glasses come in a cat-eye shape called Capri and a rounder lens called Nova. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses start at $449. The Meta-branded Gen 3 glasses are also on sale now for $299. Muse Charm For folks who don't wear glasses, Meta has teased a new product altogether: the Muse Charm. Zuckerberg says it's the “fastest way to talk to your Muse,” referring to the company's AI agent, and show it the world around you. That likely means it has a camera on the back. Zuckerberg says Meta still needs to finalize the hardware, but plans to have it ready by the holiday season. Meta Ray-Ban Display Meta's Display glasses are also getting some updates. With the implementation of Meta AI, users can create photorealistic holograms of their faces, which can be helpful for video calls.

sources.title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
passages: Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday.

Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse.
These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life.

While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent.
Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta Platforms Inc. is expanding its smart-glasses lineup with camera-free models, support for the popular new Muse assistant and a hearing-aid mode.
At its Connect conference Wednesday, the social media giant unveiled the Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first pair of glasses without cameras.

Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles.
The Meta-branded Gen 3 glasses are also on sale now for $299.
Meta says the VR Glasses cost $1,300 and will ship in the spring of 2027.
A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica.
Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform.
They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3.
The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now.
Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions.

These Meta-branded glasses come in a cat-eye shape called Capri and a rounder lens called Nova.

sources.title: Meta VR Glasses, Ray-Ban Meta Audio, Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: Specs, Features, Prices
passages: Its popular Meta Ray-Ban glasses are now in their third generation, but two new models steal the show: a powerful, slimmed-down version of Meta's Quest headsets capable of virtual and augmented reality modes, and a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban–branded smart glasses, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio.
Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles.
The Meta-branded Gen 3 glasses are also on sale now for $299.
Meta says the VR Glasses cost $1,300 and will ship in the spring of 2027.
A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica.
Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform.
They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3.
The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now.
Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions.
Muse Charm For folks who don't wear glasses, Meta has teased a new product altogether: the Muse Charm.
These Meta-branded glasses come in a cat-eye shape called Capri and a rounder lens called Nova.

extraction.body: Its popular Meta Ray-Ban glasses are now in their third generation, but two new models steal the show: a powerful, slimmed-down version of Meta's Quest headsets capable of virtual and augmented reality modes, and a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban–branded smart glasses, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform. Meta VR Glasses The next evolution of Meta’s Quest VR headset is something truly different. Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles. They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3. They sit on the nose, right in front of your face like glasses, with no headstrap needed. They look and feel more like the virtual display glasses made by companies like Viture, and what Xreal’s Project Aura seems to be shaping up to be—lightweight mixed-reality lenses that let you access virtual spaces without the burden of a VR headset. There are no included controllers, though the device can connect to Meta’s previous Quest controllers or gamepads like an Xbox controller. Form a fist and flick your thumb up or down to scroll the screen. Small prescription lens inserts can be magnetically clipped inside the lenses. (Meta has not shared how much those will cost.) The software is the same that runs on Meta’s Quest VR devices, so movie and game titles in the Quest ecosystem will work on the VR Glasses. The VR Glasses can also display a virtual keyboard on a surface in front of you, then use the embedded cameras to track specific finger placements. The only immediate downside compared to other VR headsets—at least that I could tell from a brief demo at Meta Connect—is that the VR glasses don’t cover your entire field of vision, so it doesn’t feel as immersive as a traditional VR headset. Meta says the VR Glasses cost $1,300 and will ship in the spring of 2027. Ray-Ban Meta Audio Meta has spent the past few months being absolutely pummeled by controversy about the privacy issues inherent in its camera-enabled smart glasses. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses have all the audio capabilities of a standard pair of Meta’s smart glasses, minus image and video capture. At 43 grams, they’re also lighter than the others. They come in 23 different color and style options, including the retro Ray-Ban Clubmaster frame and a more rectangular Burbank. The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 Meta's flagship line of smart glasses is getting a “Gen 3” upgrade. They have 12-MP cameras, like last year, plus 3K Dolby Atmos–enabled video capture. The glasses will get up to nine hours of battery life, two more than their predecessors. A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica. Earlier this summer, Meta debuted smart glasses under its own branding, which cost a little less but were functionally identical to the Ray-Ban models. Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions. These Meta-branded glasses come in a cat-eye shape called Capri and a rounder lens called Nova. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses start at $449. The Meta-branded Gen 3 glasses are also on sale now for $299. Muse Charm For folks who don't wear glasses, Meta has teased a new product altogether: the Muse Charm. Zuckerberg says it's the “fastest way to talk to your Muse,” referring to the company's AI agent, and show it the world around you. That likely means it has a camera on the back. Zuckerberg says Meta still needs to finalize the hardware, but plans to have it ready by the holiday season. Meta Ray-Ban Display Meta's Display glasses are also getting some updates. With the implementation of Meta AI, users can create photorealistic holograms of their faces, which can be helpful for video calls.

sources.title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
passages: Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday.

Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse.
These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life.

While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent.
Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with.

The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner.

The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data.

extraction.body: Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349. While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained. This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods. “Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses. Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours. They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed. The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted. Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life. The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said. All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse. The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data. sources.title: Meta's $1,300 VR Glasses Look Like The Vision Pro Sequel Apple Should Be Making - engadget.com
passages: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

sources.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
passages: That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.
