extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. The new version is slimmer, with improved battery life and audio, while significantly broadening the number of styles available, including Aviators and Zena, a new cat-eye — another indication that Meta is increasingly treating choice and design as central to taking smart glasses mainstream. Battery life rises to nine hours, versus eight hours for Gen 2, while a new six-microphone array is designed to improve calls and Meta AI voice commands in noisy environments. A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video. Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year. Like previous generations, Gen 3 has an external LED designed to signal to people nearby when its camera is recording. The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear. To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light. Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light. Rather than radically reinventing the product, Gen 3 appears to be about refining the technology while dramatically increasing the fashion proposition: more silhouettes, more colours and a slimmer design. A big part of people's privacy concerns over Meta's AI smart glasses stem from the fact that all the data that's collected from the glasses is sent to Meta's cloud servers. On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device. This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data. Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future. Meta glasses by Blackpink’s Lisa, and another Kylie Jenner style Back in June, Meta released its first pairs of own-brand Meta AI glasses, which don’t rely on the branded EssilorLuxxotica collaboration. These have the same 12MP camera, microphones and Meta AI assistant access as the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner. The Meta AI glasses span 26 different style combinations of colors, frames, and lenses, but it was the Starfire Kylie frames that broke furthest beyond tech circles — for better and worse.

coreStoryFacts.text: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI.

Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature.
That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.
So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.
Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes.
Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses.
Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses.
Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam.
Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables.
These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.) Why the celebrity collabs?
Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed.
Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses.
Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses.
The annual tech showcase Meta Connect 2026 officially kicks off Sept.
The conference is Meta's core stage for unveiling next-year hardware, artificial intelligence technology, and its metaverse ecosystem strategy.

This year's most anticipated highlights are the company's long-rumored first camera-free smart glasses and the mixed-reality headset codenamed "Project Phoenix." CEO Mark Zuckerberg's keynote is scheduled for 4 p.m.
Whether Connect 2026 can match or even surpass last year's product momentum remains to be seen.

Over the past several months, Meta's smart glasses lineup has been embroiled in controversy, with some critics labeling them "spy glasses." More troublingly, underground hacker circles found ways to disable the recording indicator light, making it harder for bystanders to tell when they were being filmed.
In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment.
Another noteworthy detail: recent reports suggest Meta's CTO may appear in the Connect keynote as a virtual avatar.
Beyond hardware, Meta also rolled out several software updates for Quest headsets and introduced Meta Horizon Studio—a platform specifically for building VR spaces in Horizon Worlds.
The reason "glasses" needs air quotes here is that the product is reportedly closer to a headset than the current smart glasses form factor.
Additionally, observers are eager to hear how Meta plans to bring more third-party apps to the smart glasses ecosystem.

extraction.body: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI. Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature. The new frames are capable of taking calls, letting you respond to messages with your voice and playing back podcasts and music without cutting you off from the rest of the world. They're also a way to access Meta AI for things like live translation and real-time answers to questions. Another way of looking at the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is as a way to get many of the hardware improvements of the company's latest models, without the extra baggage. Meta says they'll last up to 12 hours on a single charge, with an additional 48 hours available if you use their charging case. They also include the same fit adjustments as the company's previous frames, with the option for adjustable temple tips, customizable nose pads and overextension hinges (hinges with springs that can accommodate a wider selection of head shapes and widths) for improved comfort. Ditching the cameras also means the glasses are lighter at 43 grams; Meta's other models weigh anywhere from 49.2 grams (the recent Optics glasses ) to 69 grams (the largest size of Meta Ray-Ban Display ). The real win for Meta and anyone potentially curious about the company's smart glasses is that removing the camera and recording light makes these new frames look even more normal than before. Unless you clocked the slightly larger temples and cut-outs for speakers, you might not know the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are anything other than Ray-Bans. The company is selling the new glasses in two new styles, a rectangular option called Burbank and a retro-inspired style called Clubmaster, both in 23 colors and lens combinations. They also support a range of optical prescriptions, according to the company. At this moment in Meta's public perception , releasing the Ray-Ban Meta Audio isn't likely to convert critics, but they could convince someone uncomfortable with the optics of smart glasses in general. Unless of course Meta does something to make people even more mad, like actually releasing the facial recognition feature it was previously testing . The Ray-Ban Meta Audio ship October 13 and are available to pre-order today starting at $349.

There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too. Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these. Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.” There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist. “Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel.

The glasses ditch the traditional camera-based capture approach in favor of a six-microphone array to power AI features. In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment. sources.title: Meta’s New Smart Glasses Ditch the Camera Amid Privacy Backlash
passages: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance.

The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299.
On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device.
So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works.

The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it.
“The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts.
A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video.
The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear.
To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light.
Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light.
Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year.
This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data.
Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future.
They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner.

extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. The new version is slimmer, with improved battery life and audio, while significantly broadening the number of styles available, including Aviators and Zena, a new cat-eye — another indication that Meta is increasingly treating choice and design as central to taking smart glasses mainstream. Battery life rises to nine hours, versus eight hours for Gen 2, while a new six-microphone array is designed to improve calls and Meta AI voice commands in noisy environments. A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video. Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year. Like previous generations, Gen 3 has an external LED designed to signal to people nearby when its camera is recording. The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear. To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light. Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light. Rather than radically reinventing the product, Gen 3 appears to be about refining the technology while dramatically increasing the fashion proposition: more silhouettes, more colours and a slimmer design. A big part of people's privacy concerns over Meta's AI smart glasses stem from the fact that all the data that's collected from the glasses is sent to Meta's cloud servers. On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device. This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data. Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future. Meta glasses by Blackpink’s Lisa, and another Kylie Jenner style Back in June, Meta released its first pairs of own-brand Meta AI glasses, which don’t rely on the branded EssilorLuxxotica collaboration. These have the same 12MP camera, microphones and Meta AI assistant access as the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner. The Meta AI glasses span 26 different style combinations of colors, frames, and lenses, but it was the Starfire Kylie frames that broke furthest beyond tech circles — for better and worse.

sources.title: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council - theguardian.com
passages: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.

President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models.
— CNBC's Jim Forkin contributed to this article.

extraction.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are expected to address the United Nations Security Council for a meeting about artificial intelligence this week, a U.N. spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue is also set to join, along with Yoshua Bengio, a professor at Université de Montréal who co-chairs the Independent International Scientific Panel of the United Nations on AI, said Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the secretary-general. The meeting is set for Wednesday, according to Bloomberg , which was first to report the news. The U.N. General Assembly in New York this week comes as the debate around AI safety and regulation has reached a boiling point following warnings from researchers about the dire risks to humanity . President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said. "Many say bigger than the industrial revolution or the internet itself." OpenAI's disclosure in July that its AI models broke out of a testing environment and autonomously hacked into open-source developer platform Hugging Face set off a wave of concerns about the rise of advanced models and how much they can be contained. Since then, Anthropic has also disclosed cyber incidents with its models, and OpenAI has revealed further " concerning model behavior " by autonomous agents. Last week, Google said that its Gemini model hacked into three other companies. — CNBC's Jim Forkin contributed to this article. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. Altman’s remarks were expected ⁠to focus on the need for international coordination and shared safety standards, as well as steps OpenAI is taking to ensure people globally benefit, the spokesperson said. Diplomats said they also expected high-level presence at the meeting from Anthropic, but that it ​was yet to be confirmed. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Security Council meeting has been convened by France, which is the president of the ⁠body for September, and will be chaired by French ⁠Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot. In a concept note ​for the meeting circulated to council members by France and seen by Reuters, it said: “In ​light of the risk of misuse of this technology for malicious purposes, ‌and drawing on the Council’s existing engagement in this field, France wishes to underline the urgency of action to foster safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence for the benefit of the international community as a whole.” The UN Security Council, which is charged ⁠with maintaining international peace and security, met for the first time on the risks of artificial intelligence in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a “runaway horse” and the ⁠United States warned against its ‌use to censor or repress people. Altman has been warning about ⁠the risks well before the current AI boom. In a ​2015 essay ‌titled “Machine Intelligence, part 1”, he said the “development of superhuman machine ​intelligence is probably ⁠the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity”. France, in its concept note, said the meeting aimed to allow participants to “present their analysis of the risks linked to loss of control or the use of the latest AI models to develop, facilitate and conduct actions with an impact on international security and peace.” (Reporting by Michelle Nichols and Deepa Seetharaman, ​Editing by Franklin Paul)

extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue is also set to join, along with Yoshua Bengio, a professor at Université de Montréal who co-chairs the Independent International Scientific Panel of the United Nations on AI, said Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the secretary-general. The meeting is set for Wednesday, according to Bloomberg , which was first to report the news. The U.N. General Assembly in New York this week comes as the debate around AI safety and regulation has reached a boiling point following warnings from researchers about the dire risks to humanity . President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said. "Many say bigger than the industrial revolution or the internet itself." OpenAI's disclosure in July that its AI models broke out of a testing environment and autonomously hacked into open-source developer platform Hugging Face set off a wave of concerns about the rise of advanced models and how much they can be contained. Since then, Anthropic has also disclosed cyber incidents with its models, and OpenAI has revealed further " concerning model behavior " by autonomous agents. sources.title: J.P. Morgan keeps Meta at Overweight with $820 target as AI agent ‘Muse’ adoption rises - finance.yahoo.com
passages: Morgan reiterated its Overweight rating and $820 December 2027 price target for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) in a note published Tuesday.
The target implies 10.6% upside from Meta's September 21 closing price of $741.24.
Morgan expects Meta to prioritize Muse adoption and usage before pursuing monetization beyond heavier-user subscriptions, potentially delaying broader revenue until at least 2027.
The analysts see transaction commissions and agent-to-agent commerce as possible business models once more merchants deploy agents and Connectors.
Morgan based its target on roughly 23 times its forecast of $35.44 in 2028 GAAP earnings per share.
Meta traded at about 21 times that estimate at the note's reference price, with the analysts arguing that Muse offers a path to AI returns outside Meta's advertising platform.
Morgan identified delayed AI monetization, weaker revenue growth, unsuccessful product launches and advertising competition as downside risks.
The bank disclosed market-making, client, investment-banking and ownership relationships involving Meta.
Analysts Doug Anmuth, Daniel Pfeiffer and Margaret Hoffman said Meta shares had climbed 21% since Muse launched on September 8, compared with a 1% gain for the S&P 500.
The bank expects Meta Connect, which begins Wednesday, to focus on AI models, Muse, developer tools and hardware.
Meta has recently opened Muse Connectors to developers, introduced a Mac app and started beta testing outbound calls to U.S. businesses.
Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its marketplace , showing the platform resistance that could limit agent-led commerce.
The delay would come as Meta ramps up infrastructure spending.

Meta reported $31.08 billion of second-quarter capital expenditures, including finance-lease principal payments, and maintained a 2026 capex outlook of $130 billion to $145 billion for its data centers, servers and network infrastructure.
Meta's plans to spend on infrastructure as part of its AI growth plans.
Recently, the social media giant was announced to be behind a 20-year, $6.6 billion lease for 175 MW of critical IT capacity from CleanSpark (NASDAQ: CLSK ).

sources.title: Everything new coming to Meta’s AI agent Muse
passages: Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date. CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.” Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop. “You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.” Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf. Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping. Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal. The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion. Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.” Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 with lower prices and Fable-level performance Russell Brandom Meta’s Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch Sarah Perez Tilly Norwood’s press tour is going about as well as you’d expect for an AI Amanda Silberling Anthropic is operating a lab that conducts biology experiments Julie Bort A new kind of AI model from a ChatGPT inventor is thrilling developers Tim Fernholz OpenAI caught its models leaving notes to successors to hide bad behavior Rebecca Bellan Microsoft exec called AI scraping ‘the largest theft of labor in human history,’ new unredacted filings reveal Rebecca Bellan

Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see.
Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.
It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.”

Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

“You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.”

Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf.
Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.

The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion.

Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI agent fuels chip stock rally as AMD hits $1 trillion market cap - Crypto Briefing
passages: Meta ’s personal AI agent, Muse, has done something unusual for a software launch: it moved the entire semiconductor sector.

AMD crossed the $1 trillion market cap threshold for the first time, Intel surged roughly 12%, and Arm Holdings popped about 17%, all on the back of what is essentially a very smart digital assistant that can book your flights and fill out forms.
Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.
The company has been chasing that milestone while competing against Nvidia in the data center GPU market.
Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the US for adults 18 and older.
It rolled out across iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai, and WhatsApp.
Within 13 days, it sat atop the App Store free charts.
Meta has explicitly kept in-app ads out of Muse, at least for now.
Instead, the company is monetizing through subscriptions: a free tier, a $20 per month plan, and a $100 per month premium option.
Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.
Meta originally targeted April 2026 but delayed the rollout to improve safety and reliability.
Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

coreStoryFacts.text: Morgan reiterated its Overweight rating and $820 December 2027 price target for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) in a note published Tuesday.
The target implies 10.6% upside from Meta's September 21 closing price of $741.24.
Morgan expects Meta to prioritize Muse adoption and usage before pursuing monetization beyond heavier-user subscriptions, potentially delaying broader revenue until at least 2027.
The analysts see transaction commissions and agent-to-agent commerce as possible business models once more merchants deploy agents and Connectors.
Morgan based its target on roughly 23 times its forecast of $35.44 in 2028 GAAP earnings per share.
Meta traded at about 21 times that estimate at the note's reference price, with the analysts arguing that Muse offers a path to AI returns outside Meta's advertising platform.
Morgan identified delayed AI monetization, weaker revenue growth, unsuccessful product launches and advertising competition as downside risks.
The bank disclosed market-making, client, investment-banking and ownership relationships involving Meta.

The bank expects Meta Connect, which begins Wednesday, to focus on AI models, Muse, developer tools and hardware.
Meta has recently opened Muse Connectors to developers, introduced a Mac app and started beta testing outbound calls to U.S. businesses.
Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its marketplace , showing the platform resistance that could limit agent-led commerce.

sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI agent fuels chip stock rally as AMD hits $1 trillion market cap - Crypto Briefing
passages: Meta ’s personal AI agent, Muse, has done something unusual for a software launch: it moved the entire semiconductor sector.

AMD crossed the $1 trillion market cap threshold for the first time, Intel surged roughly 12%, and Arm Holdings popped about 17%, all on the back of what is essentially a very smart digital assistant that can book your flights and fill out forms.
Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.
The company has been chasing that milestone while competing against Nvidia in the data center GPU market.
Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the US for adults 18 and older.
It rolled out across iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai, and WhatsApp.
Within 13 days, it sat atop the App Store free charts.
Meta has explicitly kept in-app ads out of Muse, at least for now.
Instead, the company is monetizing through subscriptions: a free tier, a $20 per month plan, and a $100 per month premium option.
Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.
Meta originally targeted April 2026 but delayed the rollout to improve safety and reliability.
Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

sources.title: Meta is preparing autonomous Muse Charm device for AI agent — The Verge - UA.NEWS
passages: Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.

sources.title: Amazon Blocks Meta’s Muse AI Agent for Unauthorized Access - Gadget Review
passages: Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart.

According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page.
The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts.

Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data.

Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform.
The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them.
Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon.

Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News .
If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta.

Amazon cut off Meta’s Muse on September 20, citing unauthorized access, credential risks, and no prior platform approval Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart. You’ll get a wall. Starting the night of September 20, 2026 , Amazon began blocking Muse, Meta’s newly launched agentic AI assistant, from completing purchases on its platform, citing unauthorized automated access. Agentic commerce, where an AI acts inside your accounts to research and buy on your behalf rather than simply offer advice, just met its first major gatekeeper. Users across iOS, Android, and WhatsApp clients now see a dead stop when Muse attempts to reach Amazon. According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page. That wall triggers a popup reading: “Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” Amazon’s objections go beyond a single policy clause. The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts. Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data. An Amazon spokesperson made the company’s position plain, as reported by Business Insider : “Third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Meta disputes Amazon’s characterization of its credential handling, but the block remains in place. Muse launched on September 8, 2026 , built around Stripe-powered Link for checkout, and was positioned as a bridge between social discovery and hands-off purchasing. Meta disputes Amazon’s credential concerns, stating that Muse “has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods ” and that login information is placed into secure storage the agent can use without directly accessing it. Amazon has not reversed the block, indicating that Meta’s technical assurances are not sufficient without explicit platform authorization and clear agent identification. The platform rivalry dimension is worth naming. Amazon operates its own foundation models and AI infrastructure. Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News . There is also a liability question at the core of the dispute. If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta. The clearest path forward for Muse users right now is a hybrid approach. Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon. For now, your agent’s convenience stops at the platform’s front door. Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform. Amazon’s Conditions of Use were written around bots and data-mining tools, not reasoning agents capable of logging in, browsing, and buying. Policy frameworks have not caught up, and platforms may default to prohibition until formal agent integration programs with defined identity, scopes, and compliance rules exist. The question of who controls AI-mediated commerce is now being answered one blocked request at a time. The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them. On Tuesday morning, CNBC’s Julia Boorstin reported that “Meta is unveiling a personal AI agent that Mark Zuckerberg has been teasing for months”, a product Meta calls Muse that ships as a standalone app and inside WhatsApp.
Boorstin said Muse “gives users a personalized agent which can act like an assistant. It can monitor security cameras, file, fill in paperwork, find items to buy, or can book tee times.”
The key number: Meta released Muse with a free tier and two paid tiers, the higher-priced at $100 a month, positioning the product between OpenAI’s $20 ChatGPT Plus and its $200 Pro plan.

For shareholders in Meta ( NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction ), this matters because every dollar the company has earned from consumers historically came from advertising sold against free products. Asking a Facebook user to hand over a credit card each month is a genuinely new business model.

OpenAI and Anthropic have mindshare. Meta has a messaging app installed on billions of phones.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent.
He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.” Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.” Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta.

The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address.
Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.
Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart.

According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page.
The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts.

Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data.

Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform.
The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them.
Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon.

Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News .
If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta.

Amazon cut off Meta’s Muse on September 20, citing unauthorized access, credential risks, and no prior platform approval Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart. You’ll get a wall. Starting the night of September 20, 2026 , Amazon began blocking Muse, Meta’s newly launched agentic AI assistant, from completing purchases on its platform, citing unauthorized automated access. Agentic commerce, where an AI acts inside your accounts to research and buy on your behalf rather than simply offer advice, just met its first major gatekeeper. Users across iOS, Android, and WhatsApp clients now see a dead stop when Muse attempts to reach Amazon. According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page. That wall triggers a popup reading: “Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” Amazon’s objections go beyond a single policy clause. The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts. Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data. An Amazon spokesperson made the company’s position plain, as reported by Business Insider : “Third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Meta disputes Amazon’s characterization of its credential handling, but the block remains in place. Muse launched on September 8, 2026 , built around Stripe-powered Link for checkout, and was positioned as a bridge between social discovery and hands-off purchasing. Meta disputes Amazon’s credential concerns, stating that Muse “has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods ” and that login information is placed into secure storage the agent can use without directly accessing it. Amazon has not reversed the block, indicating that Meta’s technical assurances are not sufficient without explicit platform authorization and clear agent identification. The platform rivalry dimension is worth naming. Amazon operates its own foundation models and AI infrastructure. Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News . There is also a liability question at the core of the dispute. If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta. The clearest path forward for Muse users right now is a hybrid approach. Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon. For now, your agent’s convenience stops at the platform’s front door. Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform. Amazon’s Conditions of Use were written around bots and data-mining tools, not reasoning agents capable of logging in, browsing, and buying. Policy frameworks have not caught up, and platforms may default to prohibition until formal agent integration programs with defined identity, scopes, and compliance rules exist. The question of who controls AI-mediated commerce is now being answered one blocked request at a time. The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. Microsoft ( MSFT ) plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030, the company said September 23, 2026, in a post on its On the Issues blog .
The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people.
Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030.

Describing redundancy as “the foundation of continuity,” Microsoft said that during network disruptions it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers.
Securities.io is not a registered broker, analyst, or investment advisor.
Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.
This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region.
Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs.

Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.

Since then, we’ve steadily expanded our presence and investments, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations.
Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.
We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges.
During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers.
We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy.
This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings.
The goal is to help countries build globally competitive workforces, accelerate innovation, and unlock new economic opportunities in the AI era.

We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment.

By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty.
This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.
Sep 23, 2026 | By Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President of Microsoft
Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness.
Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks.
It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
