extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. extraction.body: Microsoft ( MSFT ) plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030, the company said September 23, 2026, in a post on its On the Issues blog . The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people. Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Under the technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, building on existing work with HUMAIN , G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. The company cited digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. Microsoft said the partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported where relevant and available by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield. Microsoft said it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. The company said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. Describing redundancy as “the foundation of continuity,” Microsoft said that during network disruptions it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said that as it expands cloud and AI infrastructure in the four countries it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, guided by the company’s global goals on carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems. Microsoft said it will also work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities for responsible water stewardship across the region and will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative built around digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs intended to help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The company said conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty, and that it will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy. The company will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, complemented by its sovereign-cloud portfolio. Microsoft also said it is deepening partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in the four countries, and that a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in the four countries will help governments connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Microsoft said it will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. The company’s AI for Good Lab will continue regional research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. Existing programs cited by the company include Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Microsoft said it will also partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. Microsoft said it has been part of the region’s journey for more than 35 years and is committed to being a partner for the long term. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative

Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.
We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity

Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience.
We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation

As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries.

A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion

Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.

We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond.
We will advance AI for Good research and innovation

Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond.
We will prepare the next generation for the AI economy

We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy. That is why Microsoft will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030.

This work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. This work builds on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
We will help education communities prepare learners for the AI era

Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities.
We will help empower workers in the AI economy
We will support local and national AI talent priorities across the Middle East

Microsoft is partnering with governments, academic institutions, and civil society organizations to support national talent priorities by advancing AI skills, leadership development, and workforce readiness programs for public-sector leaders, students, underrepresented talent, and people across the Middle East. The goal is to help countries build globally competitive workforces, accelerate innovation, and unlock new economic opportunities in the AI era.

extraction.body: Feds know of 5 crashes where cars using comma.ai devices hit slow or stopped vehicles. Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously. Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier. (Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.) Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016 . Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves . At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system. Now, Comma says the Comma Four can add lane centering, adaptive cruise, and a cloud-based dash cam to more than 325 models of car across 27 different brands. More than 30,000 drivers are using openpilot, with more than 402 million miles (650 million km) driven. But NHTSA isn’t sure that Comma’s systems are able to adequately detect a slow or stopped car in the path of travel. At least two of the five crashes involved a comma.ai-controlled car hitting a stopped vehicle; in one case, it was a first responder’s vehicle, and the resulting crash killed three. Another of the five crashes saw a comma.ai-controlled car hit a vehicle that was merging, hence this preliminary evaluation. NHTSA says it is also interested in which version of the software was running at the time of each crash—at least two involved forks of the main build, including the fatal crash, which was running a version called FrogPilot . extraction.body: A device that promises hands-off driving for cars people already own is under federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a preliminary investigation on September 21 into devices made by Comma AI, the startup founded by security hacker George Hotz, who is no longer managing day-to-day operations but remains a major owner. Regulators said vehicles equipped with the devices struck slow-moving or stopped vehicles in their lanes. Eleven people were injured, and three people died across the five reported crashes, according to the Office of Defects Investigation. "ODI has confirmed that the systems were powered on or engaged in multiple crashes," NHTSA wrote. "Preliminary data reviewed by ODI suggests that the comma system may not have adequately detected or responded to the in-lane vehicles." Authorities also plan to determine what kind of software was running during each crash, adding that some vehicles may have used modified versions, known as forks, of Comma AI's open-source software. The software in question involves comma three, comma 3X, comma four, and OpenPilot. Comma AI sells an aftermarket device that brings its driver-assistance system to more than 325 car models. The company's website states that the system can steer, accelerate, and brake, and said that it "can drive for hours without intervention." The website also tells drivers to stay alert and ready to take control at any time, and includes a driver-monitoring system that alerts when it detects driver distraction. One crash described in the NHTSA reporting appears to match a February incident in Louisiana. A state police report said a Toyota RAV4 hit an unoccupied police vehicle that was stopped in a highway lane with its emergency lights on, and two passengers in the Toyota died. The police did not identify the driving software in their account of the crash. Other autonomous driving systems and companies have faced investigations over the past few years. NHTSA in 2021 investigated Tesla's Autopilot and said that Teslas using the system struck vehicles stopped at first-responder scenes. There is also an open investigation into Waymo for striking a child near a school in Santa Monica. In July, NHTSA also issued a broader warning to driverless-vehicle developers about vehicles entering emergency scenes or blocking ambulances and firefighters. Comma AI's own support information lists stationary vehicles in the same lane among conditions that can affect OpenPilot's adaptive cruise control. Comma AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

extraction.body: Feds know of 5 crashes where cars using comma.ai devices hit slow or stopped vehicles. Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously. Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier. (Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.) Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016 . Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves . At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system. Now, Comma says the Comma Four can add lane centering, adaptive cruise, and a cloud-based dash cam to more than 325 models of car across 27 different brands. More than 30,000 drivers are using openpilot, with more than 402 million miles (650 million km) driven. But NHTSA isn’t sure that Comma’s systems are able to adequately detect a slow or stopped car in the path of travel. At least two of the five crashes involved a comma.ai-controlled car hitting a stopped vehicle; in one case, it was a first responder’s vehicle, and the resulting crash killed three. Another of the five crashes saw a comma.ai-controlled car hit a vehicle that was merging, hence this preliminary evaluation. NHTSA says it is also interested in which version of the software was running at the time of each crash—at least two involved forks of the main build, including the fatal crash, which was running a version called FrogPilot . extraction.body: A device that promises hands-off driving for cars people already own is under federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a preliminary investigation on September 21 into devices made by Comma AI, the startup founded by security hacker George Hotz, who is no longer managing day-to-day operations but remains a major owner. Regulators said vehicles equipped with the devices struck slow-moving or stopped vehicles in their lanes. Eleven people were injured, and three people died across the five reported crashes, according to the Office of Defects Investigation. "ODI has confirmed that the systems were powered on or engaged in multiple crashes," NHTSA wrote. "Preliminary data reviewed by ODI suggests that the comma system may not have adequately detected or responded to the in-lane vehicles." Authorities also plan to determine what kind of software was running during each crash, adding that some vehicles may have used modified versions, known as forks, of Comma AI's open-source software. The software in question involves comma three, comma 3X, comma four, and OpenPilot. Comma AI sells an aftermarket device that brings its driver-assistance system to more than 325 car models. The company's website states that the system can steer, accelerate, and brake, and said that it "can drive for hours without intervention." The website also tells drivers to stay alert and ready to take control at any time, and includes a driver-monitoring system that alerts when it detects driver distraction. One crash described in the NHTSA reporting appears to match a February incident in Louisiana. A state police report said a Toyota RAV4 hit an unoccupied police vehicle that was stopped in a highway lane with its emergency lights on, and two passengers in the Toyota died. The police did not identify the driving software in their account of the crash. Other autonomous driving systems and companies have faced investigations over the past few years. NHTSA in 2021 investigated Tesla's Autopilot and said that Teslas using the system struck vehicles stopped at first-responder scenes. There is also an open investigation into Waymo for striking a child near a school in Santa Monica. In July, NHTSA also issued a broader warning to driverless-vehicle developers about vehicles entering emergency scenes or blocking ambulances and firefighters. Comma AI's own support information lists stationary vehicles in the same lane among conditions that can affect OpenPilot's adaptive cruise control. Comma AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a preliminary investigation on September 21 into devices made by Comma AI, the startup founded by security hacker George Hotz, who is no longer managing day-to-day operations but remains a major owner.
Regulators said vehicles equipped with the devices struck slow-moving or stopped vehicles in their lanes.
Eleven people were injured, and three people died across the five reported crashes, according to the Office of Defects Investigation.
"ODI has confirmed that the systems were powered on or engaged in multiple crashes," NHTSA wrote.

"Preliminary data reviewed by ODI suggests that the comma system may not have adequately detected or responded to the in-lane vehicles." Authorities also plan to determine what kind of software was running during each crash, adding that some vehicles may have used modified versions, known as forks, of Comma AI's open-source software.
The software in question involves comma three, comma 3X, comma four, and OpenPilot.
Comma AI sells an aftermarket device that brings its driver-assistance system to more than 325 car models.

The company's website states that the system can steer, accelerate, and brake, and said that it "can drive for hours without intervention." The website also tells drivers to stay alert and ready to take control at any time, and includes a driver-monitoring system that alerts when it detects driver distraction.
One crash described in the NHTSA reporting appears to match a February incident in Louisiana.
A state police report said a Toyota RAV4 hit an unoccupied police vehicle that was stopped in a highway lane with its emergency lights on, and two passengers in the Toyota died.
The police did not identify the driving software in their account of the crash.
Other autonomous driving systems and companies have faced investigations over the past few years.
NHTSA in 2021 investigated Tesla's Autopilot and said that Teslas using the system struck vehicles stopped at first-responder scenes.
There is also an open investigation into Waymo for striking a child near a school in Santa Monica.
In July, NHTSA also issued a broader warning to driverless-vehicle developers about vehicles entering emergency scenes or blocking ambulances and firefighters.
Comma AI's own support information lists stationary vehicles in the same lane among conditions that can affect OpenPilot's adaptive cruise control.
Comma AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

sources.title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app
passages: The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling.
YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.
YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails.
Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best.
Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.

At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences.
The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.
Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.
YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.

extraction.body: YouTube has unveiled a host of new features for its content creation platform, YouTube Studio. The updates are aimed at making the creative journey easier and more efficient for creators. The new tools include Ask Studio, an AI-powered feature that provides quick insights on video performance and community feedback. It also includes an Inspiration tab to spark creativity with suggested topics, title testing for optimizing video titles and thumbnails, and advanced auto dubbing, among other features. The Ask Studio feature is designed to answer creators' most pressing questions about their content. It can provide insights into analytics, community engagement, and offer new ideas for future videos. The Inspiration tab, on the other hand, helps creators brainstorm by suggesting topics based on audience behavior. The latest update also includes a feature for creators to collaborate on videos. Up to five collaborators can be added to one video, which will be shown to all participating creators' audiences. Additionally, YouTube is improving its auto-dubbing capabilities with new lip sync technology for translated videos across 20 languages. YouTube is also expanding its likeness detection tool to all creators in the YouTube Partner Program. This technology enables creators to detect, manage, and request the removal of unauthorized videos using their facial likeness. The move is part of YouTube's commitment to building AI technology that responsibly empowers human creativity while protecting creators and their businesses from potential misuse or misrepresentation.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.
Similar glitches were reported in isolated Reddit threads and creator communities in mid-March.YouTube has not issued an official statement specifically addressing Monday's reports as of press time.

For smaller channels and full-time creators, even brief outages can create stress, especially when real-time analytics are unavailable during peak viewing hours.Monday's issues appeared less severe than the March 10 event, which affected loading across both mobile and desktop for many users simultaneously.

Geographic distribution of complaints suggested possible regional variations, though a clear pattern was not immediately evident.YouTube, owned by Google, has expanded its creator tools significantly in recent years to support the platform's more than 2.5 billion monthly users and millions of active channels.

A few shared screenshots showing missing analytics or error screens, urging YouTube to improve communication during technical difficulties.For those unable to access Studio, alternative methods include using third-party analytics tools (where compliant with YouTube's terms) or waiting for mobile app updates.

YouTube periodically rolls out updates to the Studio app that can temporarily introduce or resolve bugs.Looking ahead, industry analysts expect continued enhancements to creator tools, including deeper AI integration for content optimization and monetization insights.
Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.
On March 10, the platform experienced a widespread partial outage that prevented many creators from accessing their dashboards, triggering panic among some who feared channel termination notices.
YouTube later confirmed the issue was fixed, restoring normal access and accurate statistics.
YouTube's massive scale — processing billions of hours of video daily — makes maintaining 100% uptime a complex engineering challenge.Creators offered mixed reactions online.

While the main YouTube platform for viewers appeared largely unaffected, the creator tools that allow uploading, editing metadata, checking performance and managing channels experienced intermittent disruptions.Downdetector and other outage-tracking sites showed a modest uptick in reports for YouTube-related problems, though not at the scale of major past outages.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

Any disruption draws swift attention because it directly impacts income for those monetizing through ads, memberships, Super Chats and merchandise.Industry observers note that YouTube's rapid feature rollout and heavy reliance on machine learning systems can occasionally lead to backend strain.

Even short disruptions can cascade into lost opportunities, particularly for live streamers or those timing content releases around trending topics.As of Monday afternoon, no widespread confirmation of a full outage had emerged from YouTube.

extraction.body: YouTube has unveiled a host of new features for its content creation platform, YouTube Studio. The updates are aimed at making the creative journey easier and more efficient for creators. The new tools include Ask Studio, an AI-powered feature that provides quick insights on video performance and community feedback. It also includes an Inspiration tab to spark creativity with suggested topics, title testing for optimizing video titles and thumbnails, and advanced auto dubbing, among other features. The Ask Studio feature is designed to answer creators' most pressing questions about their content. It can provide insights into analytics, community engagement, and offer new ideas for future videos. The Inspiration tab, on the other hand, helps creators brainstorm by suggesting topics based on audience behavior. The latest update also includes a feature for creators to collaborate on videos. Up to five collaborators can be added to one video, which will be shown to all participating creators' audiences. Additionally, YouTube is improving its auto-dubbing capabilities with new lip sync technology for translated videos across 20 languages. YouTube is also expanding its likeness detection tool to all creators in the YouTube Partner Program. This technology enables creators to detect, manage, and request the removal of unauthorized videos using their facial likeness. The move is part of YouTube's commitment to building AI technology that responsibly empowers human creativity while protecting creators and their businesses from potential misuse or misrepresentation.

passages: Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing.
At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.
Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.
Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before.
Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support.
Users will be able to download and watch movies.
The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience.
Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.
These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.

So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”

passages: In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset.
Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas.
Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9.

A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles.
The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.
The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets.
Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

extraction.body: Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie. Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor. “We are… self-aware,” she sighed. A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror. They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest. The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap. The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces. Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting. In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing. But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works. The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through. The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. The novelty will probably wear off after a while, but at first, it’s pretty thrilling if you’ve never used this kind of technology before — which appears to be the target market for Meta VR Glasses. Of course, there’s a work capability too; you can mirror your Mac or PC into this virtual space, either wirelessly or via USB-C. On the other hand, the device’s $1,299.99 price tag — more than a solid TV and Blu-ray player combined — might be a deterrent to the average consumer who hasn’t yet dipped their toe into VR. That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer. The only way to be remotely convinced of the technology is to experience it for yourself, which a re-creation on a flat screen (say, a YouTube video) can’t fully convey. There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled. There are kinks that still need to be worked out by launch, like the glare from light sources behind you leaking into your field of view (perhaps the one downside to opening up those goggles), but a head tilt here or there can probably solve that issue. Also not part of the tech demo was the ability to re-orient where exactly in your horizontal field of view a given screen appears, but this was something Meta’s engineers demonstrated for us on the fly, with the promise that we’d eventually be able to do it ourselves. Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby. Look, it can be hard to trust big tech in our increasingly dystopian world, and who knows what data this particular chapter of the company will try to harness or sell. But the lineup of streaming services and viewing features on offer makes Meta VR Glasses one of the more intriguing developments in the field if you’re unsure about stepping into virtual spaces. Compared to existing devices on the market, the openness of the design — which still allows you to peek out from time to time and go back to the real world pretty easily — makes for the kind of compromise that fence-sitters like myself might just be able to accept. passages: Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie. Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.

“We are… self-aware,” she sighed. A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror.

They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest.

The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap.

The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces.

Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting.

In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing.

But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works.

The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.

The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. coreStoryFacts.text: Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing.
At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.
Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.
Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before.
Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support.
Users will be able to download and watch movies.
The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience.
Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.
These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.

So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”

The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.
The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets.
Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

extraction.body: Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie. Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor. “We are… self-aware,” she sighed. A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror. They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest. The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap. The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces. Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting. In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing. But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works. The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through. The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. The novelty will probably wear off after a while, but at first, it’s pretty thrilling if you’ve never used this kind of technology before — which appears to be the target market for Meta VR Glasses. Of course, there’s a work capability too; you can mirror your Mac or PC into this virtual space, either wirelessly or via USB-C. On the other hand, the device’s $1,299.99 price tag — more than a solid TV and Blu-ray player combined — might be a deterrent to the average consumer who hasn’t yet dipped their toe into VR. That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer. The only way to be remotely convinced of the technology is to experience it for yourself, which a re-creation on a flat screen (say, a YouTube video) can’t fully convey. There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled. There are kinks that still need to be worked out by launch, like the glare from light sources behind you leaking into your field of view (perhaps the one downside to opening up those goggles), but a head tilt here or there can probably solve that issue. Also not part of the tech demo was the ability to re-orient where exactly in your horizontal field of view a given screen appears, but this was something Meta’s engineers demonstrated for us on the fly, with the promise that we’d eventually be able to do it ourselves. Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby. Look, it can be hard to trust big tech in our increasingly dystopian world, and who knows what data this particular chapter of the company will try to harness or sell. But the lineup of streaming services and viewing features on offer makes Meta VR Glasses one of the more intriguing developments in the field if you’re unsure about stepping into virtual spaces. Compared to existing devices on the market, the openness of the design — which still allows you to peek out from time to time and go back to the real world pretty easily — makes for the kind of compromise that fence-sitters like myself might just be able to accept. If nothing else, it’s more convenient, and slightly less embarrassing, than buying a scalped IMAX ticket on eBay.

sources.title: Gov. JB Pritzker assembling Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess AI threats - Chicago Sun-Times
passages: The Democratic governor signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess “the various risks posed by Al to the safety of Illinois residents and the critical infrastructure residents rely on.”

JB Pritzker is convening a panel of experts to advise state officials on the potential threats of artificial intelligence as a growing number of industry leaders warn the burgeoning, self-improving technology could spell doomsday for humanity if left unchecked.

Pritzker will name his AI Cabinet members “in the coming weeks” to work alongside numerous state agency leaders, including from the Department of Innovation and Technology, the Department of Public Health and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency.
“Illinois has already enacted nation-leading laws that hold Big Tech accountable and today I’m taking executive action to keep this a priority,” Pritzker said.

They’re expected to come from backgrounds in academia, law, ethics and governance, and provide recommendations on potential public safety threats, protecting public assets and evaluating possible regulations, according to Pritzker’s office.
From WBUR and NPR, co-hosted by Robin Young and Scott Tong, with news from Chicago from WBEZ’s Lisa Labuz.
