extraction.body: Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here . Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD. In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°). That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable. Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply. Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical. As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup. Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content. While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S. Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more. Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot. When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand. Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there. At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300.

While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here .

Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD.

In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°).

That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable.

Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply.
Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical.

As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup.

Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content.

While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S.

Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more.

Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot.

When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand.

story.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses

facts.text: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.
That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

It also sounds like the next one will be something a little different.UploadVR reported that Meta's next head-worn VR device might launch in 2026, but it likely won't be a big, bulky VR headset like we're used to seeing from Quest devices.

While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset.
You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here .

As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD.
It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup.

The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect.
Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon.
Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display .
There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI.

extraction.body: There's a lot for Mark Zuckerberg to cover at this year's keynote. Meta is about to hold its biggest event of the year. While Connect was once solely dedicated to virtual reality, the event now covers all the company's hardware projects, as well as AI and the metaverse. And this year could be even more jam-packed than usual. Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover. Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 . There will be additional talks and developer sessions the following day, starting with a 10AM PT/1PM ET "developer state of the union." As usual, I'll be on the ground watching the keynote live from Meta's HQ in Menlo Park so check back for our liveblog and post-keynote coverage. In the meantime, here's everything I'll be looking out for during Connect. As with the last few years, there's likely to be a lot of glasses-related news. One interesting change with this year's strategy is that the company is reportedly working on a pair of camera-free frames . These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant. The lack of cameras could offer Meta a couple of advantages. The frames will reportedly be a bit slimmer and look more like "normal glasses." More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses. Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others. In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect. Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon. That could be a reference to these camera-free frames or, perhaps, a new Gen 3 lineup (the first Gen 2 models debuted at last year's Connect). Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display . There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI. But it's been a while since we've heard anything about the rumored device, sometimes called "Hypernova 2," so Meta could be holding that one back for now. It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect. Several images of the lightweight device recently surfaced in a HorizonOS update. Those images show a thin device that almost looks more like a pair of goggles than a headset. It also clearly shows a cable, which supports previous reporting that Phoenix will rely on a tethered connection to a separate puck. It's also rumored to support hand and eye tracking rather than a dedicated controller. And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year. Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors. A new kind of headset will probably also mean some updates to HorizonOS, and it will be interesting to see what kinds of experiences Meta will promote alongside the new hardware. The company has been shuttering VR studios left and right, so I doubt we would see any huge game announcements to go with Phoenix. But it does seem like Meta could promote more entertainment-focused offerings. Deadline reported last year that Meta was backing a new "3D horror series" based on A24's Talk to Me that's apparently meant for viewing in the company's headsets. We may also hear more about Meta's holographic avatars that we first saw two years ago with its Orion prototype. Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility. The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote. These avatars could also factor into Meta's evolving vision for the metaverse. When the company almost shut down Horizon Worlds in VR earlier this year, Bosworth said that augmented reality was very much part of the company's "expansive construct of the metaverse." The last few years of Connect have included a lot of AI news and this year shouldn't be any different. This will be the first Connect since we've seen a flood of new AI releases from the company's superintelligence group, and I'm sure the company is saving some AI-focused updates for Connect. I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse . The company teased that glasses support for the agent would be coming "soon," so I wouldn't be surprised if we hear more about how this will work at Connect. (Agent capabilities could also be a good selling point for camera-free glasses.) I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem. Last year at Connect, the company announced a handful of apps that would be coming to its camera glasses, but we haven't seen a whole lot of momentum since. And earlier this year it started allowing developers to create dedicated apps for Meta Ray-Ban Display. Showing off a new slate of third-party apps for the frames could be a good way to build more excitement for the product even if we don't see updated hardware.

extraction.body: As Meta’s Threads marks its first anniversary on July 6, one thing is clear: the social media platform is far from the 'Twitter killer' it set out to be. Despite amassing 175 million monthly active users, Threads cannot yet boast the same vibrancy as the popular micro-blogging platform, now called X. Nowhere is this more profound than in India, one of the biggest markets for social media platforms.The Meta India team had feared this. In fact, in the lead-up to the launch last year, on July 6, 2023, they had expressed their apprehensions to the Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the Threads' core team, The New Indian Express has learnt. They were not heeded.'Poorly executed'"We were very unhappy with the product -- its viability, the lacklustreness of its functions, and its hurried, overnight launch," said a Meta India insider who was part of the Threads team. The plan was to capitalise on the unrest at Twitter after Elon Musk's takeover and the growing resentment towards some of his proposals, such as the introduction of subscriptions."Indeed. The months prior saw Musk, the new CEO of Twitter, fire most of the employees, rename the platform X, restore previously banned accounts, introduce fees and firewalls, and overhaul the algorithm and content moderation policies. It was a time of much upheaval at Twitter and Zuckerberg hoped to ride this wave."A smart business move, no doubt, but poorly executed," the source added. Though the India team had warned their counterparts in the US, Zuckerberg's instructions were to press on. In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products. Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries. Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok. It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves. It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey. Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads. "We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut. I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later. Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications. No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram. The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram. Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing. In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge. Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said. However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet. "For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character. It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm. "I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about. And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point. "Threads didn't bring anything new to the table. No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram. Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family. This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads. What is after all one year in the life of a digital product? However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular. "It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted. Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

extraction.body: There's a lot for Mark Zuckerberg to cover at this year's keynote. Meta is about to hold its biggest event of the year. While Connect was once solely dedicated to virtual reality, the event now covers all the company's hardware projects, as well as AI and the metaverse. And this year could be even more jam-packed than usual. Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover. Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 . There will be additional talks and developer sessions the following day, starting with a 10AM PT/1PM ET "developer state of the union." As usual, I'll be on the ground watching the keynote live from Meta's HQ in Menlo Park so check back for our liveblog and post-keynote coverage. In the meantime, here's everything I'll be looking out for during Connect. As with the last few years, there's likely to be a lot of glasses-related news. One interesting change with this year's strategy is that the company is reportedly working on a pair of camera-free frames . These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant. The lack of cameras could offer Meta a couple of advantages. The frames will reportedly be a bit slimmer and look more like "normal glasses." More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses. Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others. In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect. Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon. That could be a reference to these camera-free frames or, perhaps, a new Gen 3 lineup (the first Gen 2 models debuted at last year's Connect). Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display . There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI. But it's been a while since we've heard anything about the rumored device, sometimes called "Hypernova 2," so Meta could be holding that one back for now. It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect. Several images of the lightweight device recently surfaced in a HorizonOS update. Those images show a thin device that almost looks more like a pair of goggles than a headset. It also clearly shows a cable, which supports previous reporting that Phoenix will rely on a tethered connection to a separate puck. It's also rumored to support hand and eye tracking rather than a dedicated controller. And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year. Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors. A new kind of headset will probably also mean some updates to HorizonOS, and it will be interesting to see what kinds of experiences Meta will promote alongside the new hardware. The company has been shuttering VR studios left and right, so I doubt we would see any huge game announcements to go with Phoenix. But it does seem like Meta could promote more entertainment-focused offerings. Deadline reported last year that Meta was backing a new "3D horror series" based on A24's Talk to Me that's apparently meant for viewing in the company's headsets. We may also hear more about Meta's holographic avatars that we first saw two years ago with its Orion prototype. Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility. The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote. These avatars could also factor into Meta's evolving vision for the metaverse. When the company almost shut down Horizon Worlds in VR earlier this year, Bosworth said that augmented reality was very much part of the company's "expansive construct of the metaverse." The last few years of Connect have included a lot of AI news and this year shouldn't be any different. This will be the first Connect since we've seen a flood of new AI releases from the company's superintelligence group, and I'm sure the company is saving some AI-focused updates for Connect. I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse . The company teased that glasses support for the agent would be coming "soon," so I wouldn't be surprised if we hear more about how this will work at Connect. (Agent capabilities could also be a good selling point for camera-free glasses.) I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem. Last year at Connect, the company announced a handful of apps that would be coming to its camera glasses, but we haven't seen a whole lot of momentum since. And earlier this year it started allowing developers to create dedicated apps for Meta Ray-Ban Display. Showing off a new slate of third-party apps for the frames could be a good way to build more excitement for the product even if we don't see updated hardware.

extraction.body: As Meta’s Threads marks its first anniversary on July 6, one thing is clear: the social media platform is far from the 'Twitter killer' it set out to be. Despite amassing 175 million monthly active users, Threads cannot yet boast the same vibrancy as the popular micro-blogging platform, now called X. Nowhere is this more profound than in India, one of the biggest markets for social media platforms.The Meta India team had feared this. In fact, in the lead-up to the launch last year, on July 6, 2023, they had expressed their apprehensions to the Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the Threads' core team, The New Indian Express has learnt. They were not heeded.'Poorly executed'"We were very unhappy with the product -- its viability, the lacklustreness of its functions, and its hurried, overnight launch," said a Meta India insider who was part of the Threads team. The plan was to capitalise on the unrest at Twitter after Elon Musk's takeover and the growing resentment towards some of his proposals, such as the introduction of subscriptions."Indeed. The months prior saw Musk, the new CEO of Twitter, fire most of the employees, rename the platform X, restore previously banned accounts, introduce fees and firewalls, and overhaul the algorithm and content moderation policies. It was a time of much upheaval at Twitter and Zuckerberg hoped to ride this wave."A smart business move, no doubt, but poorly executed," the source added. Though the India team had warned their counterparts in the US, Zuckerberg's instructions were to press on. In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products. Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries. Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok. It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves. It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey. Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads. "We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut. I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later. Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications. No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram. The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram. Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing. In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge. Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said. However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet. "For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character. It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm. "I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about. And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point. "Threads didn't bring anything new to the table. No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram. Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family. This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads. What is after all one year in the life of a digital product? However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular. "It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted. Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

extraction.body: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI. Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature. The new frames are capable of taking calls, letting you respond to messages with your voice and playing back podcasts and music without cutting you off from the rest of the world. They're also a way to access Meta AI for things like live translation and real-time answers to questions. Another way of looking at the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is as a way to get many of the hardware improvements of the company's latest models, without the extra baggage. Meta says they'll last up to 12 hours on a single charge, with an additional 48 hours available if you use their charging case. They also include the same fit adjustments as the company's previous frames, with the option for adjustable temple tips, customizable nose pads and overextension hinges (hinges with springs that can accommodate a wider selection of head shapes and widths) for improved comfort. Ditching the cameras also means the glasses are lighter at 43 grams; Meta's other models weigh anywhere from 49.2 grams (the recent Optics glasses ) to 69 grams (the largest size of Meta Ray-Ban Display ). The real win for Meta and anyone potentially curious about the company's smart glasses is that removing the camera and recording light makes these new frames look even more normal than before. Unless you clocked the slightly larger temples and cut-outs for speakers, you might not know the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are anything other than Ray-Bans. The company is selling the new glasses in two new styles, a rectangular option called Burbank and a retro-inspired style called Clubmaster, both in 23 colors and lens combinations. They also support a range of optical prescriptions, according to the company. At this moment in Meta's public perception , releasing the Ray-Ban Meta Audio isn't likely to convert critics, but they could convince someone uncomfortable with the optics of smart glasses in general. Unless of course Meta does something to make people even more mad, like actually releasing the facial recognition feature it was previously testing . The Ray-Ban Meta Audio ship October 13 and are available to pre-order today starting at $349.

extraction.body: Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern. Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making. “Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.” [Image: There are multiple combinations of colors and lenses across two styles for the audio-only glasses. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.” The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too. Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these. Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options. Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.) Why the celebrity collabs? “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.” There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. AI in your frames All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist. “Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel.

extraction.body: The annual tech showcase Meta Connect 2026 officially kicks off Sept. 23–24 U.S. Eastern time. The conference is Meta's core stage for unveiling next-year hardware, artificial intelligence technology, and its metaverse ecosystem strategy. This year's most anticipated highlights are the company's long-rumored first camera-free smart glasses and the mixed-reality headset codenamed "Project Phoenix." CEO Mark Zuckerberg's keynote is scheduled for 4 p.m. Pacific time on Sept. 23 (7 p.m. EDT on Sept. 23, 7 a.m. Taipei time on Sept. 24). Meta said anyone can register on the company's official website to watch the livestream for free—just provide a name, email address, and country. The Meta for Developers Facebook page will also stream simultaneously. Live translation will be available for non-English-speaking viewers during the broadcast. Day two's developer sessions and technical talks begin at 1 p.m. EDT, with technical sessions available on demand afterward. On the hardware front, the biggest story isn't a simple spec bump but a shift in product direction. According to The Information , Meta is expected to unveil its first camera-free smart glasses at this year's conference, internally codenamed "Luna." The glasses ditch the traditional camera-based capture approach in favor of a six-microphone array to power AI features. In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment. Meta's mainstream smart glasses all currently include built-in cameras—so why launch a camera-free version? The market consensus is that this isn't merely about creating a budget-friendly product, but a direct response to growing public privacy concerns. Over the past several months, Meta's smart glasses lineup has been embroiled in controversy, with some critics labeling them "spy glasses." More troublingly, underground hacker circles found ways to disable the recording indicator light, making it harder for bystanders to tell when they were being filmed. Meta has already taken multiple steps to address these criticisms. The company patched the vulnerability hackers exploited, so users can no longer bypass the recording indicator. It also automatically disables camera functionality when the system detects that the blinking LED indicator has been covered with tape or clip-on accessories. Instagram has begun banning users who upload videos of themselves interacting with others while wearing tampered glasses. The launch of camera-free smart glasses can be seen as Meta's latest move in the privacy-protection direction. Beyond smart glasses, Meta may also use this conference to formally unveil the long-rumored "Project Phoenix" mixed-reality device. The reason "glasses" needs air quotes here is that the product is reportedly closer to a headset than the current smart glasses form factor. The device is expected to feature a goggle-style design—or, put another way, it looks more like a pair of "bulky glasses." Even so, Phoenix is expected to be more portable, lighter, and more practical than Meta's previous Quest-series VR headsets. Reports indicate Phoenix may rely on an external "compute module" to handle complex processing, thereby reducing the weight of the headset itself. At the same time, it can run the same HorizonOS operating system as the Quest lineup. Users could get the best of both worlds: high-quality mixed-reality content without having to wear a heavy headset for extended periods. Earlier this month, a new batch of images of the device circulated online, further raising the likelihood of an official announcement at this conference. That said, this slimmer mixed-reality device may not necessarily ship this year. While Meta Connect's focus will likely land on hardware, AI technology iteration and ecosystem upgrades remain core highlights of the keynote—especially with Meta's new personal AI agent Muse having just opened to the public earlier this month. Meta is expected to reveal more details about Muse during the conference. The company may also unveil a new version of its flagship Llama large language model, which has been quiet since its April 2025 update and is eagerly anticipated by the industry. The integration prospects between Muse and Meta's wearable devices are equally compelling. Meta has previously teased that the agent will "soon" support smart glasses, and the conference will likely detail the specific integration approach. Conversely, AI agent capabilities could become a major selling point for Meta's smart glasses going forward. Additionally, observers are eager to hear how Meta plans to bring more third-party apps to the smart glasses ecosystem. At last year's Connect, Meta announced several apps coming to smart glasses, but follow-through has been sparse. Earlier this year, Meta opened up permissions allowing developers to build dedicated apps for the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses. Even without hardware updates, showcasing a slate of new third-party apps tailored for smart glasses could effectively boost consumer anticipation. Any discussion of a new headset inevitably leads to the HorizonOS system updates Meta may bring alongside it. According to sources, Meta may announce a new version of HorizonOS at the conference to improve usability. On the content side, Meta has recently shut down several VR studios, so observers don't expect major game announcements to accompany the Phoenix device. However, Meta may push more entertainment-focused content. Sources indicate Meta is producing a new 3D horror series based on the film Talk to Me , designed specifically for viewing inside its own headsets. Another noteworthy detail: recent reports suggest Meta's CTO may appear in the Connect keynote as a virtual avatar. This kind of avatar application is part of Meta's evolving metaverse vision. Looking back at Connect 2025, Meta launched multiple smart glasses in one go, including the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta, the sports-oriented Oakley Meta Vanguards, and the company's first AI glasses with a built-in display, the Meta Ray-Ban Display. Beyond hardware, Meta also rolled out several software updates for Quest headsets and introduced Meta Horizon Studio—a platform specifically for building VR spaces in Horizon Worlds. Whether Connect 2026 can match or even surpass last year's product momentum remains to be seen. From camera-free smart glasses to a mixed-reality headset, to the ecosystem integration of Muse AI and the Llama large language model, Meta is attempting to strike a new balance between privacy controversies and technological innovation. CEO Mark Zuckerberg's keynote is scheduled for 4 p.m. Pacific time on Sept. 23 (7 p.m. EDT on Sept. 23, 7 a.m. Taipei time on Sept. 24).

Meta said anyone can register on the company's official website to watch the livestream for free—just provide a name, email address, and country. The Meta for Developers Facebook page will also stream simultaneously. Live translation will be available for non-English-speaking viewers during the broadcast. Day two's developer sessions and technical talks begin at 1 p.m. EDT, with technical sessions available on demand afterward.

On the hardware front, the biggest story isn't a simple spec bump but a shift in product direction. According to The Information , Meta is expected to unveil its first camera-free smart glasses at this year's conference, internally codenamed "Luna." The glasses ditch the traditional camera-based capture approach in favor of a six-microphone array to power AI features. In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment.

Meta's mainstream smart glasses all currently include built-in cameras—so why launch a camera-free version? The market consensus is that this isn't merely about creating a budget-friendly product, but a direct response to growing public privacy concerns. Over the past several months, Meta's smart glasses lineup has been embroiled in controversy, with some critics labeling them "spy glasses." More troublingly, underground hacker circles found ways to disable the recording indicator light, making it harder for bystanders to tell when they were being filmed.

Meta has already taken multiple steps to address these criticisms. The company patched the vulnerability hackers exploited, so users can no longer bypass the recording indicator. It also automatically disables camera functionality when the system detects that the blinking LED indicator has been covered with tape or clip-on accessories. Instagram has begun banning users who upload videos of themselves interacting with others while wearing tampered glasses. The launch of camera-free smart glasses can be seen as Meta's latest move in the privacy-protection direction.

Beyond smart glasses, Meta may also use this conference to formally unveil the long-rumored "Project Phoenix" mixed-reality device. The reason "glasses" needs air quotes here is that the product is reportedly closer to a headset than the current smart glasses form factor. The device is expected to feature a goggle-style design—or, put another way, it looks more like a pair of "bulky glasses."

Even so, Phoenix is expected to be more portable, lighter, and more practical than Meta's previous Quest-series VR headsets. Reports indicate Phoenix may rely on an external "compute module" to handle complex processing, thereby reducing the weight of the headset itself. At the same time, it can run the same HorizonOS operating system as the Quest lineup. Users could get the best of both worlds: high-quality mixed-reality content without having to wear a heavy headset for extended periods. Earlier this month, a new batch of images of the device circulated online, further raising the likelihood of an official announcement at this conference. That said, this slimmer mixed-reality device may not necessarily ship this year.

While Meta Connect's focus will likely land on hardware, AI technology iteration and ecosystem upgrades remain core highlights of the keynote—especially with Meta's new personal AI agent Muse having just opened to the public earlier this month. Meta is expected to reveal more details about Muse during the conference. The company may also unveil a new version of its flagship Llama large language model, which has been quiet since its April 2025 update and is eagerly anticipated by the industry.

The integration prospects between Muse and Meta's wearable devices are equally compelling. Meta has previously teased that the agent will "soon" support smart glasses, and the conference will likely detail the specific integration approach. Conversely, AI agent capabilities could become a major selling point for Meta's smart glasses going forward.

Additionally, observers are eager to hear how Meta plans to bring more third-party apps to the smart glasses ecosystem. At last year's Connect, Meta announced several apps coming to smart glasses, but follow-through has been sparse. Earlier this year, Meta opened up permissions allowing developers to build dedicated apps for the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses. Even without hardware updates, showcasing a slate of new third-party apps tailored for smart glasses could effectively boost consumer anticipation.

Any discussion of a new headset inevitably leads to the HorizonOS system updates Meta may bring alongside it. According to sources, Meta may announce a new version of HorizonOS at the conference to improve usability.

On the content side, Meta has recently shut down several VR studios, so observers don't expect major game announcements to accompany the Phoenix device. However, Meta may push more entertainment-focused content. Sources indicate Meta is producing a new 3D horror series based on the film Talk to Me , designed specifically for viewing inside its own headsets.

Another noteworthy detail: recent reports suggest Meta's CTO may appear in the Connect keynote as a virtual avatar. This kind of avatar application is part of Meta's evolving metaverse vision. Looking back at Connect 2025, Meta launched multiple smart glasses in one go, including the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta, the sports-oriented Oakley Meta Vanguards, and the company's first AI glasses with a built-in display, the Meta Ray-Ban Display. Beyond hardware, Meta also rolled out several software updates for Quest headsets and introduced Meta Horizon Studio—a platform specifically for building VR spaces in Horizon Worlds.

Whether Connect 2026 can match or even surpass last year's product momentum remains to be seen. From camera-free smart glasses to a mixed-reality headset, to the ecosystem integration of Muse AI and the Llama large language model, Meta is attempting to strike a new balance between privacy controversies and technological innovation.

extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. The new version is slimmer, with improved battery life and audio, while significantly broadening the number of styles available, including Aviators and Zena, a new cat-eye — another indication that Meta is increasingly treating choice and design as central to taking smart glasses mainstream. Battery life rises to nine hours, versus eight hours for Gen 2, while a new six-microphone array is designed to improve calls and Meta AI voice commands in noisy environments. A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video. Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year. Like previous generations, Gen 3 has an external LED designed to signal to people nearby when its camera is recording. The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear. To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light. Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light. Rather than radically reinventing the product, Gen 3 appears to be about refining the technology while dramatically increasing the fashion proposition: more silhouettes, more colours and a slimmer design. A big part of people's privacy concerns over Meta's AI smart glasses stem from the fact that all the data that's collected from the glasses is sent to Meta's cloud servers. On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device. This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data. Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future. Meta glasses by Blackpink’s Lisa, and another Kylie Jenner style Back in June, Meta released its first pairs of own-brand Meta AI glasses, which don’t rely on the branded EssilorLuxxotica collaboration. These have the same 12MP camera, microphones and Meta AI assistant access as the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner. The Meta AI glasses span 26 different style combinations of colors, frames, and lenses, but it was the Starfire Kylie frames that broke furthest beyond tech circles — for better and worse.

extraction.body: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI. Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature. The new frames are capable of taking calls, letting you respond to messages with your voice and playing back podcasts and music without cutting you off from the rest of the world. They're also a way to access Meta AI for things like live translation and real-time answers to questions. Another way of looking at the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is as a way to get many of the hardware improvements of the company's latest models, without the extra baggage. Meta says they'll last up to 12 hours on a single charge, with an additional 48 hours available if you use their charging case. They also include the same fit adjustments as the company's previous frames, with the option for adjustable temple tips, customizable nose pads and overextension hinges (hinges with springs that can accommodate a wider selection of head shapes and widths) for improved comfort. Ditching the cameras also means the glasses are lighter at 43 grams; Meta's other models weigh anywhere from 49.2 grams (the recent Optics glasses ) to 69 grams (the largest size of Meta Ray-Ban Display ). The real win for Meta and anyone potentially curious about the company's smart glasses is that removing the camera and recording light makes these new frames look even more normal than before. Unless you clocked the slightly larger temples and cut-outs for speakers, you might not know the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are anything other than Ray-Bans. The company is selling the new glasses in two new styles, a rectangular option called Burbank and a retro-inspired style called Clubmaster, both in 23 colors and lens combinations. They also support a range of optical prescriptions, according to the company. At this moment in Meta's public perception , releasing the Ray-Ban Meta Audio isn't likely to convert critics, but they could convince someone uncomfortable with the optics of smart glasses in general. Unless of course Meta does something to make people even more mad, like actually releasing the facial recognition feature it was previously testing . The Ray-Ban Meta Audio ship October 13 and are available to pre-order today starting at $349.

There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too. extraction.body: The annual tech showcase Meta Connect 2026 officially kicks off Sept. 23–24 U.S. Eastern time. The conference is Meta's core stage for unveiling next-year hardware, artificial intelligence technology, and its metaverse ecosystem strategy. This year's most anticipated highlights are the company's long-rumored first camera-free smart glasses and the mixed-reality headset codenamed "Project Phoenix." CEO Mark Zuckerberg's keynote is scheduled for 4 p.m. Pacific time on Sept. 23 (7 p.m. EDT on Sept. 23, 7 a.m. Taipei time on Sept. 24). Meta said anyone can register on the company's official website to watch the livestream for free—just provide a name, email address, and country. The Meta for Developers Facebook page will also stream simultaneously. Live translation will be available for non-English-speaking viewers during the broadcast. Day two's developer sessions and technical talks begin at 1 p.m. EDT, with technical sessions available on demand afterward. On the hardware front, the biggest story isn't a simple spec bump but a shift in product direction. According to The Information , Meta is expected to unveil its first camera-free smart glasses at this year's conference, internally codenamed "Luna." The glasses ditch the traditional camera-based capture approach in favor of a six-microphone array to power AI features. In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment. Meta's mainstream smart glasses all currently include built-in cameras—so why launch a camera-free version? The market consensus is that this isn't merely about creating a budget-friendly product, but a direct response to growing public privacy concerns. Over the past several months, Meta's smart glasses lineup has been embroiled in controversy, with some critics labeling them "spy glasses." More troublingly, underground hacker circles found ways to disable the recording indicator light, making it harder for bystanders to tell when they were being filmed. Meta has already taken multiple steps to address these criticisms. The company patched the vulnerability hackers exploited, so users can no longer bypass the recording indicator. It also automatically disables camera functionality when the system detects that the blinking LED indicator has been covered with tape or clip-on accessories. Instagram has begun banning users who upload videos of themselves interacting with others while wearing tampered glasses. The launch of camera-free smart glasses can be seen as Meta's latest move in the privacy-protection direction. Beyond smart glasses, Meta may also use this conference to formally unveil the long-rumored "Project Phoenix" mixed-reality device. The reason "glasses" needs air quotes here is that the product is reportedly closer to a headset than the current smart glasses form factor. The device is expected to feature a goggle-style design—or, put another way, it looks more like a pair of "bulky glasses." Even so, Phoenix is expected to be more portable, lighter, and more practical than Meta's previous Quest-series VR headsets. Reports indicate Phoenix may rely on an external "compute module" to handle complex processing, thereby reducing the weight of the headset itself. At the same time, it can run the same HorizonOS operating system as the Quest lineup. Users could get the best of both worlds: high-quality mixed-reality content without having to wear a heavy headset for extended periods. Earlier this month, a new batch of images of the device circulated online, further raising the likelihood of an official announcement at this conference. That said, this slimmer mixed-reality device may not necessarily ship this year. While Meta Connect's focus will likely land on hardware, AI technology iteration and ecosystem upgrades remain core highlights of the keynote—especially with Meta's new personal AI agent Muse having just opened to the public earlier this month. Meta is expected to reveal more details about Muse during the conference. The company may also unveil a new version of its flagship Llama large language model, which has been quiet since its April 2025 update and is eagerly anticipated by the industry. The integration prospects between Muse and Meta's wearable devices are equally compelling. Meta has previously teased that the agent will "soon" support smart glasses, and the conference will likely detail the specific integration approach. Conversely, AI agent capabilities could become a major selling point for Meta's smart glasses going forward. Additionally, observers are eager to hear how Meta plans to bring more third-party apps to the smart glasses ecosystem. At last year's Connect, Meta announced several apps coming to smart glasses, but follow-through has been sparse. Earlier this year, Meta opened up permissions allowing developers to build dedicated apps for the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses. Even without hardware updates, showcasing a slate of new third-party apps tailored for smart glasses could effectively boost consumer anticipation. Any discussion of a new headset inevitably leads to the HorizonOS system updates Meta may bring alongside it. According to sources, Meta may announce a new version of HorizonOS at the conference to improve usability. On the content side, Meta has recently shut down several VR studios, so observers don't expect major game announcements to accompany the Phoenix device. However, Meta may push more entertainment-focused content. Sources indicate Meta is producing a new 3D horror series based on the film Talk to Me , designed specifically for viewing inside its own headsets. Another noteworthy detail: recent reports suggest Meta's CTO may appear in the Connect keynote as a virtual avatar. This kind of avatar application is part of Meta's evolving metaverse vision. Looking back at Connect 2025, Meta launched multiple smart glasses in one go, including the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta, the sports-oriented Oakley Meta Vanguards, and the company's first AI glasses with a built-in display, the Meta Ray-Ban Display. Beyond hardware, Meta also rolled out several software updates for Quest headsets and introduced Meta Horizon Studio—a platform specifically for building VR spaces in Horizon Worlds. Whether Connect 2026 can match or even surpass last year's product momentum remains to be seen. From camera-free smart glasses to a mixed-reality headset, to the ecosystem integration of Muse AI and the Llama large language model, Meta is attempting to strike a new balance between privacy controversies and technological innovation. extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. The new version is slimmer, with improved battery life and audio, while significantly broadening the number of styles available, including Aviators and Zena, a new cat-eye — another indication that Meta is increasingly treating choice and design as central to taking smart glasses mainstream. Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature.
That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.
So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.

Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses.

sources.title: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council - theguardian.com
passages: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.
