extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

extraction.body: UNITED NATIONS, Sept 18 (Reuters) – OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN ​General Assembly, an OpenAI spokesperson said on Friday. The 15-member Security Council is ‌due to meet on Wednesday on artificial intelligence and international security, just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control. “Sam Altman will brief an open ‌UN ​Security Council meeting in person next week,” an OpenAI spokesperson ⁠told Reuters. Altman’s remarks were expected ⁠to focus on the need for international coordination and shared safety standards, as well as steps OpenAI is taking to ensure people globally benefit, the spokesperson said. Diplomats said they also expected high-level presence at the meeting from Anthropic, but that it ​was yet to be confirmed. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Security Council meeting has been convened by France, which is the president of the ⁠body for September, and will be chaired by French ⁠Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot. In a concept note ​for the meeting circulated to council members by France and seen by Reuters, it said: “In ​light of the risk of misuse of this technology for malicious purposes, ‌and drawing on the Council’s existing engagement in this field, France wishes to underline the urgency of action to foster safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence for the benefit of the international community as a whole.” The UN Security Council, which is charged ⁠with maintaining international peace and security, met for the first time on the risks of artificial intelligence in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a “runaway horse” and the ⁠United States warned against its ‌use to censor or repress people. Altman has been warning about ⁠the risks well before the current AI boom. In a ​2015 essay ‌titled “Machine Intelligence, part 1”, he said the “development of superhuman machine ​intelligence is probably ⁠the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity”. France, in its concept note, said the meeting aimed to allow participants to “present their analysis of the risks linked to loss of control or the use of the latest AI models to develop, facilitate and conduct actions with an impact on international security and peace.” (Reporting by Michelle Nichols and Deepa Seetharaman, ​Editing by Franklin Paul)

extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue is also set to join, along with Yoshua Bengio, a professor at Université de Montréal who co-chairs the Independent International Scientific Panel of the United Nations on AI, said Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the secretary-general. The meeting is set for Wednesday, according to Bloomberg , which was first to report the news. The U.N. General Assembly in New York this week comes as the debate around AI safety and regulation has reached a boiling point following warnings from researchers about the dire risks to humanity . President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said. "Many say bigger than the industrial revolution or the internet itself." OpenAI's disclosure in July that its AI models broke out of a testing environment and autonomously hacked into open-source developer platform Hugging Face set off a wave of concerns about the rise of advanced models and how much they can be contained. Since then, Anthropic has also disclosed cyber incidents with its models, and OpenAI has revealed further " concerning model behavior " by autonomous agents. Last week, Google said that its Gemini model hacked into three other companies. — CNBC's Jim Forkin contributed to this article. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. Diplomats said they also expected high-level presence at the meeting from Anthropic, but that it ​was yet to be confirmed. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Security Council meeting has been convened by France, which is the president of the ⁠body for September, and will be chaired by French ⁠Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot. Altman has been warning about ⁠the risks well before the current AI boom. In a ​2015 essay ‌titled “Machine Intelligence, part 1”, he said the “development of superhuman machine ​intelligence is probably ⁠the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity”. story.title: Sam Altman’s remarks at the United Nations Security Council - OpenAI

facts.text: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are expected to address the United Nations Security Council for a meeting about artificial intelligence this week, a U.N. spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models.
— CNBC's Jim Forkin contributed to this article.

sources.title: J.P. Morgan keeps Meta at Overweight with $820 target as AI agent ‘Muse’ adoption rises - finance.yahoo.com
passages: Morgan reiterated its Overweight rating and $820 December 2027 price target for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) in a note published Tuesday.
The target implies 10.6% upside from Meta's September 21 closing price of $741.24.
Morgan expects Meta to prioritize Muse adoption and usage before pursuing monetization beyond heavier-user subscriptions, potentially delaying broader revenue until at least 2027.
The analysts see transaction commissions and agent-to-agent commerce as possible business models once more merchants deploy agents and Connectors.
Morgan based its target on roughly 23 times its forecast of $35.44 in 2028 GAAP earnings per share.
Meta traded at about 21 times that estimate at the note's reference price, with the analysts arguing that Muse offers a path to AI returns outside Meta's advertising platform.
Morgan identified delayed AI monetization, weaker revenue growth, unsuccessful product launches and advertising competition as downside risks.
The bank disclosed market-making, client, investment-banking and ownership relationships involving Meta.
Analysts Doug Anmuth, Daniel Pfeiffer and Margaret Hoffman said Meta shares had climbed 21% since Muse launched on September 8, compared with a 1% gain for the S&P 500.
The bank expects Meta Connect, which begins Wednesday, to focus on AI models, Muse, developer tools and hardware.
Meta has recently opened Muse Connectors to developers, introduced a Mac app and started beta testing outbound calls to U.S. businesses.
Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its marketplace , showing the platform resistance that could limit agent-led commerce.
The delay would come as Meta ramps up infrastructure spending.

Meta reported $31.08 billion of second-quarter capital expenditures, including finance-lease principal payments, and maintained a 2026 capex outlook of $130 billion to $145 billion for its data centers, servers and network infrastructure.
Meta's plans to spend on infrastructure as part of its AI growth plans.
Recently, the social media giant was announced to be behind a 20-year, $6.6 billion lease for 175 MW of critical IT capacity from CleanSpark (NASDAQ: CLSK ).

passages: Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date. CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.” Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop. “You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.” Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf. Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping. Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal. The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf.
Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.

The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion.

Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI agent fuels chip stock rally as AMD hits $1 trillion market cap - Crypto Briefing
passages: Meta ’s personal AI agent, Muse, has done something unusual for a software launch: it moved the entire semiconductor sector.

AMD crossed the $1 trillion market cap threshold for the first time, Intel surged roughly 12%, and Arm Holdings popped about 17%, all on the back of what is essentially a very smart digital assistant that can book your flights and fill out forms.
Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.
The company has been chasing that milestone while competing against Nvidia in the data center GPU market.
Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the US for adults 18 and older.
It rolled out across iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai, and WhatsApp.
Within 13 days, it sat atop the App Store free charts.
Meta has explicitly kept in-app ads out of Muse, at least for now.
Instead, the company is monetizing through subscriptions: a free tier, a $20 per month plan, and a $100 per month premium option.
Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.
Meta originally targeted April 2026 but delayed the rollout to improve safety and reliability.
Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

coreStoryFacts.text: Morgan reiterated its Overweight rating and $820 December 2027 price target for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) in a note published Tuesday.
The target implies 10.6% upside from Meta's September 21 closing price of $741.24.
Morgan expects Meta to prioritize Muse adoption and usage before pursuing monetization beyond heavier-user subscriptions, potentially delaying broader revenue until at least 2027.
The analysts see transaction commissions and agent-to-agent commerce as possible business models once more merchants deploy agents and Connectors.
Morgan based its target on roughly 23 times its forecast of $35.44 in 2028 GAAP earnings per share.
Meta traded at about 21 times that estimate at the note's reference price, with the analysts arguing that Muse offers a path to AI returns outside Meta's advertising platform.
Morgan identified delayed AI monetization, weaker revenue growth, unsuccessful product launches and advertising competition as downside risks.
The bank disclosed market-making, client, investment-banking and ownership relationships involving Meta.
Analysts Doug Anmuth, Daniel Pfeiffer and Margaret Hoffman said Meta shares had climbed 21% since Muse launched on September 8, compared with a 1% gain for the S&P 500.
The bank expects Meta Connect, which begins Wednesday, to focus on AI models, Muse, developer tools and hardware.
Meta has recently opened Muse Connectors to developers, introduced a Mac app and started beta testing outbound calls to U.S. businesses.
Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its marketplace , showing the platform resistance that could limit agent-led commerce.

This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.

sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI agent fuels chip stock rally as AMD hits $1 trillion market cap - Crypto Briefing
passages: Meta ’s personal AI agent, Muse, has done something unusual for a software launch: it moved the entire semiconductor sector.

AMD crossed the $1 trillion market cap threshold for the first time, Intel surged roughly 12%, and Arm Holdings popped about 17%, all on the back of what is essentially a very smart digital assistant that can book your flights and fill out forms.
Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.
The company has been chasing that milestone while competing against Nvidia in the data center GPU market.
Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the US for adults 18 and older.
It rolled out across iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai, and WhatsApp.
Within 13 days, it sat atop the App Store free charts.
Meta has explicitly kept in-app ads out of Muse, at least for now.
Instead, the company is monetizing through subscriptions: a free tier, a $20 per month plan, and a $100 per month premium option.
Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.
Meta originally targeted April 2026 but delayed the rollout to improve safety and reliability.
Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

facts.text: Morgan reiterated its Overweight rating and $820 December 2027 price target for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) in a note published Tuesday.
The target implies 10.6% upside from Meta's September 21 closing price of $741.24.
Morgan expects Meta to prioritize Muse adoption and usage before pursuing monetization beyond heavier-user subscriptions, potentially delaying broader revenue until at least 2027.
The analysts see transaction commissions and agent-to-agent commerce as possible business models once more merchants deploy agents and Connectors.
Morgan based its target on roughly 23 times its forecast of $35.44 in 2028 GAAP earnings per share.
Meta traded at about 21 times that estimate at the note's reference price, with the analysts arguing that Muse offers a path to AI returns outside Meta's advertising platform.
Morgan identified delayed AI monetization, weaker revenue growth, unsuccessful product launches and advertising competition as downside risks.
The bank disclosed market-making, client, investment-banking and ownership relationships involving Meta.
Analysts Doug Anmuth, Daniel Pfeiffer and Margaret Hoffman said Meta shares had climbed 21% since Muse launched on September 8, compared with a 1% gain for the S&P 500.
The bank expects Meta Connect, which begins Wednesday, to focus on AI models, Muse, developer tools and hardware.
Meta has recently opened Muse Connectors to developers, introduced a Mac app and started beta testing outbound calls to U.S. businesses.
Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its marketplace , showing the platform resistance that could limit agent-led commerce.
The delay would come as Meta ramps up infrastructure spending.

Meta reported $31.08 billion of second-quarter capital expenditures, including finance-lease principal payments, and maintained a 2026 capex outlook of $130 billion to $145 billion for its data centers, servers and network infrastructure.
Meta's plans to spend on infrastructure as part of its AI growth plans.
Recently, the social media giant was announced to be behind a 20-year, $6.6 billion lease for 175 MW of critical IT capacity from CleanSpark (NASDAQ: CLSK ).

There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

sources.title: Meta is preparing autonomous Muse Charm device for AI agent — The Verge - UA.NEWS
passages: Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.

sources.title: Amazon Blocks Meta’s Muse AI Agent for Unauthorized Access - Gadget Review
passages: Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart.

According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page.
The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts.

Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data.

Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform.
The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them.
Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon.

Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News .
If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta.

Amazon cut off Meta’s Muse on September 20, citing unauthorized access, credential risks, and no prior platform approval Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart. You’ll get a wall. Starting the night of September 20, 2026 , Amazon began blocking Muse, Meta’s newly launched agentic AI assistant, from completing purchases on its platform, citing unauthorized automated access. Agentic commerce, where an AI acts inside your accounts to research and buy on your behalf rather than simply offer advice, just met its first major gatekeeper. Users across iOS, Android, and WhatsApp clients now see a dead stop when Muse attempts to reach Amazon. According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page. That wall triggers a popup reading: “Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” Amazon’s objections go beyond a single policy clause. The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts. Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data. An Amazon spokesperson made the company’s position plain, as reported by Business Insider : “Third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Meta disputes Amazon’s characterization of its credential handling, but the block remains in place. Muse launched on September 8, 2026 , built around Stripe-powered Link for checkout, and was positioned as a bridge between social discovery and hands-off purchasing. Meta disputes Amazon’s credential concerns, stating that Muse “has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods ” and that login information is placed into secure storage the agent can use without directly accessing it. Amazon has not reversed the block, indicating that Meta’s technical assurances are not sufficient without explicit platform authorization and clear agent identification. The platform rivalry dimension is worth naming. Amazon operates its own foundation models and AI infrastructure. Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News . There is also a liability question at the core of the dispute. If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta. The clearest path forward for Muse users right now is a hybrid approach. Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon. For now, your agent’s convenience stops at the platform’s front door. Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform. Amazon’s Conditions of Use were written around bots and data-mining tools, not reasoning agents capable of logging in, browsing, and buying. Policy frameworks have not caught up, and platforms may default to prohibition until formal agent integration programs with defined identity, scopes, and compliance rules exist. The question of who controls AI-mediated commerce is now being answered one blocked request at a time. The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them. According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page.

Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data.

Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform.

Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon.

On Tuesday morning, CNBC’s Julia Boorstin reported that “Meta is unveiling a personal AI agent that Mark Zuckerberg has been teasing for months”, a product Meta calls Muse that ships as a standalone app and inside WhatsApp.
Boorstin said Muse “gives users a personalized agent which can act like an assistant. It can monitor security cameras, file, fill in paperwork, find items to buy, or can book tee times.”
The key number: Meta released Muse with a free tier and two paid tiers, the higher-priced at $100 a month, positioning the product between OpenAI’s $20 ChatGPT Plus and its $200 Pro plan.

For shareholders in Meta ( NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction ), this matters because every dollar the company has earned from consumers historically came from advertising sold against free products. Asking a Facebook user to hand over a credit card each month is a genuinely new business model.
The stock is not acting as the market has priced that in. META closed at $613.48 on Tuesday, down 18.19% over the last year.

Meta AI Chief Alex Wang said, “We are incredibly excited about consumer AI. And we see today a very small number of people who have really experienced the power of advanced agents in these new models.” The category is wide open, but nobody has proven consumers will pay a subscription for a personal agent at any price, let alone $100 a month.

The pricing itself signals to Wall Street that Meta is moving beyond its core story. The company has spent years telling investors AI would show up as better ad targeting, with $59.36 billion in advertising revenue in Q2.
A paid tier creates a recurring line item independent of ad load and gives Zuckerberg a way to defend the $130 to $145 billion in 2026 capital expenditure the company just guided to.
OpenAI and Anthropic have mindshare. Meta has a messaging app installed on billions of phones.

Meta ended Q2 with 3.6 billion daily active people across its family of apps, and management said WhatsApp is the leading surface where people engage with Meta AI. Business agents are the proof of concept: more than 1 million businesses already use them weekly on WhatsApp and Messenger.

Compare that to Google ( NASDAQ:GOOGL ), which reaches consumers through a Gemini App with 950 million monthly active users, and Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT ), which reaches workers through 30 million Copilot paid seats sold at roughly $30 per user per month.
WhatsApp lets Meta skip the acquisition funnel. Users don’t download anything, and payment flows through a channel they already trust.

Meta’s Q2 free cash flow collapsed to $784 million from $8.55 billion a year earlier, with capital spending hitting $31.1 billion in the quarter alone. Long-term debt climbed to $83.66 billion to fund the buildout. Full details are in the Q2 8-K .
Analysts have noticed, with 45 downward EPS revisions for fiscal 2026 in the last 30 days against only 4 upward.

A $100-a-month subscription is how Zuckerberg starts answering the return-on-invested-capital question. Even modest paid conversion across a billion-user surface would meaningfully change the revenue mix.

Alphabet is monetizing AI through Cloud, which grew 82% year over year in Q2. Microsoft is monetizing it through per-seat Copilot and Azure, which crossed $100 billion in annual revenue. Meta is the only one of the three still searching for a repeatable AI revenue line outside advertising, and the picks-and-shovels names powering all three buildouts (we rounded up seven of them in a free report on the AI infrastructure trade ) are the ones capturing the capex right now.
The stock trades at a forward P/E of 18x, a discount to Microsoft’s 27x multiple, with an analyst target of $754.77.

Muse is late to a market where ChatGPT already owns the noun. Distribution alone rarely closes a product gap, although WhatsApp is the closest thing to an unfair advantage anyone has brought to this fight.
The bear case: free cash flow is thin, capex is climbing, and consumers may not pay $100 a month for an agent that overlaps with cheaper tools they already use.
The bull case: Meta’s ad business is still growing 27%, the valuation is reasonable, and any paid AI revenue is upside the market has not underwritten.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent.
He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.” Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.” Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta.

The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address.
Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.
Try to buy something on Amazon through Meta’s Muse AI agent right now, and you won’t get a cart.

According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page.
The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts.

Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data.

Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform.
The platforms that hold the checkout infrastructure hold the leverage, and any AI agent that wants access will need to negotiate terms, not assume them.
Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon.

Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News .
If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta.

Users across iOS, Android, and WhatsApp clients now see a dead stop when Muse attempts to reach Amazon. According to GeekWire , which first reported the change, Amazon deployed an anti-bot wall , a technical barrier that prevents automated browsers from reaching the site, stopping Muse before it can even load the Amazon search page. That wall triggers a popup reading: “Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” Amazon’s objections go beyond a single policy clause. The company says Meta never notified or sought authorization before Muse accessed Amazon.com and acted inside customer accounts. Amazon also states that Muse does not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing, and that the assistant, in Amazon’s characterization, “appears to capture and store customer credentials,” raising security and privacy concerns about third-party AI access to sensitive account data. An Amazon spokesperson made the company’s position plain, as reported by Business Insider : “Third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Meta disputes Amazon’s characterization of its credential handling, but the block remains in place. Allowing a competitor’s agent to automate purchases on its platform risks losing control over user data and experience, and may preempt any native agentic shopping features Amazon plans to develop, a point noted in analysis by both GeekWire and Forkast News . There is also a liability question at the core of the dispute. If Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers absorb the returns and disputes, not Meta. The clearest path forward for Muse users right now is a hybrid approach. Current guidance suggests using Muse for product research and comparison, then completing the actual checkout manually on Amazon. For now, your agent’s convenience stops at the platform’s front door. Commentators have framed this as an early “tollgate” moment for agentic commerce: a major retailer explicitly treating a mainstream AI assistant as an unauthorized intruder and asserting the right to decide which agents can transact on its platform. Amazon’s Conditions of Use were written around bots and data-mining tools, not reasoning agents capable of logging in, browsing, and buying. Policy frameworks have not caught up, and platforms may default to prohibition until formal agent integration programs with defined identity, scopes, and compliance rules exist. The question of who controls AI-mediated commerce is now being answered one blocked request at a time. extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. We will add to our local partnerships across the region. We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges. As we look to the future, we will invest further in technology, digital resilience, and the people across the region.
From now until 2030, we will pursue the following initiatives with our partners in the region:
We will deepen our partnerships through national AI champions

Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness. This builds on work with organizations including HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait, alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait.

These partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses. They will be supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield, where relevant and available.
We will invest in subsea and terrestrial connectivity

Digital resilience depends on strong and reliable networks. Protecting subsea and terrestrial connectivity requires sustained cooperation between governments and the private sector, but the foundation of continuity is redundancy. A diverse network of high-capacity routes allows traffic to be rerouted around disruptions, minimizing latency and maintaining critical data flows.

Microsoft has helped expand both the capacity and reliability of digital connectivity across regions through investments in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, as well as operating a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers.

Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region.
We will build AI infrastructure with the planet in mind

As we expand our cloud and AI infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will do so with a focus on responsible growth. Guided by Microsoft’s global goals to address carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems, we will work with our lessor partners to ensure that the cloud infrastructure supporting our services advances Microsoft’s water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible.

Water resilience is particularly important across the Middle East. Building on Microsoft’s global experience advancing water stewardship through water reuse, replenishment, and innovative water management solutions, we will work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities that advance responsible water stewardship across the region.

As AI accelerates economic opportunity across the Middle East, expanding access to clean energy will be essential to ensuring this growth is sustainable. We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative

Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.
We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity

Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience.
We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation

As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries.

A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion

Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.

We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond.
We will advance AI for Good research and innovation

Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond.
We will prepare the next generation for the AI economy

We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy. That is why Microsoft will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030.

This work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. This work builds on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
We will help education communities prepare learners for the AI era

Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities.
We will help empower workers in the AI economy
We will support local and national AI talent priorities across the Middle East

Microsoft is partnering with governments, academic institutions, and civil society organizations to support national talent priorities by advancing AI skills, leadership development, and workforce readiness programs for public-sector leaders, students, underrepresented talent, and people across the Middle East. The goal is to help countries build globally competitive workforces, accelerate innovation, and unlock new economic opportunities in the AI era.

extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East.
