passages: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

coreStoryFacts.text: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.

AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

World leaders called for stronger international safeguards and oversight on artificial intelligence during the general debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urging stronger global coordination to manage AI risks. Guterres warned, "The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability," as U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI. French President Emmanuel Macron said, "We must build the capacity to audit these models rather than depend on a handful of private actors," while Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva criticized the concentration of technological power and warned of "a race with no ethical boundaries". South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said AI benefits could deepen inequality and imbalance "unless we are properly prepared for it," and he said South Korea would establish a global AI hub to tackle shared challenges ranging from climate change to health and food security. The debate was set to move from the General Assembly to the UN Security Council on Wednesday, when the council was scheduled to discuss AI and international security. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng does not plan to attend . Reported by 101 WIXX and BigGo Finance . Heads of major AI firms told the UN Security Council that the industry urgently needed global oversight, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warning, "If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world could "lose control of the future of AI," and he argued, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone." Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue told the council that his company had relied on a Chinese AI model to defend itself in incidents involving out-of-control AI models, saying, "We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI." The United States administration pushed back through its representative Michael Kratsios, who told members, "We totally reject all efforts by international bodies to assert centralised control and global governance of AI." Daniel Forti, head of UN Affairs at the International Crisis Group, said member states understood there would be a need for international cooperation and rules for AI even if the biggest players focused on growth opportunities. The UN debate centered on whether humans or machines should control life-and-death decisions, and it highlighted worries about AI use in warfare including machines making decisions without human control. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the Security Council that the tech leaders "are telling us in stark terms that it cannot be left to them to prevent disaster from befalling the world," and he added, "We cannot ignore them because they are right." Michael Kratsios pushed back again by saying control concerns were "not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structure," while he said, "We want you, our allies and partners, to share in the benefits of this technology." UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots," and Kentaro Toyama said, "Killer robots are technically easy to build, and they are real." The meeting also placed the issue in a wider diplomatic sequence, with the discussion unfolding as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit and as Trump was expected to meet Xi in Washington amid escalating competition between the two countries to develop and dominate the technology. passages: Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software.
It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses.
The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. SEE ALSO: Meet the Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3, starting at $249 The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. The Tamagotchi-like gadget is designed for people who don't wear Meta's smart glasses, and Zuckerberg called it the fastest way to talk to Muse without wearing them. SEE ALSO: Meet the Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3, starting at $249 The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. During a live demo, Zuckerberg used Meta's glasses to talk with his customized Muse assistant, which he'd named Agrippa, about a handheld device he was working on. That device turned out to be Muse Charm.Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Muse offers free usage alongside paid subscriptions. Zuckerberg also suggested Meta could eventually collect a small fee on transactions the assistant helps complete.Muse Charm will ship by the holidays in December, according to Zuckerberg. Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. Muse Charm's main selling point is that it runs on the same assistant as Meta's glasses.

OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will also provide richer text output, creating a more seamless experience between spoken and written interactions. Users will be able to switch between voice and text more easily within the same conversation. OpenAI later integrated GPT-Live into its desktop app, allowing users to use voice commands to complete tasks through the Work tab and build applications through Codex. The latest update brings similar capabilities to mobile devices as voice increasingly becomes a way to control AI assistants and execute multi-step tasks. OpenAI is not the only AI company focusing on smoother workflows between mobile and desktop. Anthropic has recently improved the handoff between its mobile and desktop experiences and merged its Claude Chat and Cowork interfaces into a more unified environment. OpenAI, however, continues to keep its standard chat experience and Work workspace separate.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026, in New York City. Getty Images / Michael M. Santiago President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a rebranding of the term “artificial intelligence,” saying during the United Nations General Assembly that from now on, it will be called “super intelligence.” “From this point forward, all of United States’ documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, ‘super,’ as opposed to ‘artificial’,” he said. Though the rebrand may have been a surprise to many, superintelligence is already an established term in AI literature. It was popularized in philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 bestseller Superintelligence , which defines the term as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.” Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, thus refers to future AI systems that could be much smarter than humans, and contrasts with the weaker forms of AI that exist today. ASI is a step beyond AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which OpenAI defines as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” By this definition, today’s AI isn’t AGI yet, much less ASI, since we can’t yet hire AI as a reliable virtual employee. Some experts dislike the term superintelligence, or question whether it’s a coherent concept. In the influential 2025 paper “AI as Normal Technology,” authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan write, “We do not think there is a useful sense of the term ‘intelligence’ in which AI is more intelligent than people acting with the help of AI.” But others say the possible renaming contributes to an ongoing conversation about AI’s growing abilities. “‘Super’ does align well with the fact that AI is exceeding human capabilities in a growing range of tasks and by increasing margins, which can have distinct national security implications beyond simply matching human performance,” said Caleb Withers, a research associate for the Technology and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. For example, in early September, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of the most important open problems in math. As AI becomes more capable, it has grown increasingly central to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week to discuss trade and AI issues. Bostrom, who has warned of the dangers of fully superintelligent AI systems, said an all-out AI race increases the risk that the technology gets out of control . “If competitors are convinced that coming second [in the AI race] means the total loss of everything they care about, they will take whatever risk necessary to bypass their rivals,” he said. Trump reportedly worries that an AI slowdown could cause a market crash, and sees “super intelligence” as a critical sector for America to stay ahead of China. “Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins.” NEXT STORY: NATO’s thumbs-up for AWS shows Europe still needs America

President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a rebranding of the term “artificial intelligence,” saying during the United Nations General Assembly that from now on, it will be called “super intelligence.”
“From this point forward, all of United States’ documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, ‘super,’ as opposed to ‘artificial’,” he said.

Though the rebrand may have been a surprise to many, superintelligence is already an established term in AI literature. It was popularized in philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 bestseller Superintelligence , which defines the term as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.” Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, thus refers to future AI systems that could be much smarter than humans, and contrasts with the weaker forms of AI that exist today.

ASI is a step beyond AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which OpenAI defines as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” By this definition, today’s AI isn’t AGI yet, much less ASI, since we can’t yet hire AI as a reliable virtual employee.

Some experts dislike the term superintelligence, or question whether it’s a coherent concept. In the influential 2025 paper “AI as Normal Technology,” authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan write, “We do not think there is a useful sense of the term ‘intelligence’ in which AI is more intelligent than people acting with the help of AI.”
But others say the possible renaming contributes to an ongoing conversation about AI’s growing abilities.

“‘Super’ does align well with the fact that AI is exceeding human capabilities in a growing range of tasks and by increasing margins, which can have distinct national security implications beyond simply matching human performance,” said Caleb Withers, a research associate for the Technology and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
For example, in early September, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of the most important open problems in math.

As AI becomes more capable, it has grown increasingly central to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week to discuss trade and AI issues. Bostrom, who has warned of the dangers of fully superintelligent AI systems, said an all-out AI race increases the risk that the technology gets out of control . “If competitors are convinced that coming second [in the AI race] means the total loss of everything they care about, they will take whatever risk necessary to bypass their rivals,” he said.

Trump reportedly worries that an AI slowdown could cause a market crash, and sees “super intelligence” as a critical sector for America to stay ahead of China. “Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins.”

passages: Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Chainlink (CRYPTO: LINK) both tap into the growing trend of tokenization—the shift of Treasuries, funds, and bank deposits onto blockchains.
However, as we move through 2026, ETH has declined, while LINK has risen 7%.
Chainlink, which cryptocurrency is likely to capture more market share as this trend continues to develop?

As the demand for tokenization grows, Chainlink's role expands, particularly as BlackRock's tokenized money market fund, BUIDL, currently holds about $2.8 billion across eight blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana, and Polygon.
Chainlink facilitates interactions between these ledgers, while Ethereum retains the largest volume of assets.
Ethereum's transaction model differs from Chainlink's.
Every transaction on Ethereum incurs a fee paid in ETH, part of which is burned, reducing ETH supply during high-activity periods.
Despite this mechanism, the overall ETH supply has increased by about 1% over the last year, mainly because much of the activity now occurs on layer-2 networks that pay only minimal fees to Ethereum.
Our assessment leans towards Chainlink as the stronger candidate for growth.
In contrast, Ethereum must compete with various other ledgers for the same deposits.
This is reflected in the market trends, with LINK up 7% for 2026 while ETH has remained in the red.
Both Ethereum and Chainlink performed well recently, with ETH rising by 11% to reach $2,664 and LINK climbing by 12% to $12.
What matters, though, is the broader picture, since both cryptocurrencies offer similar pitches for tokenization until you dig into the details.
Chainlink's significant partnerships further underscore its potential.
Since 2023, Swift, the network banks rely on for cross-border payments, has been testing connections with Chainlink and several major institutions, including Citi and BNP Paribas.
In August 2023, they successfully moved tokenized assets between an Ethereum test network and other blockchains.
Tom Zschach, Swift's chief innovation officer, remarked that these tests demonstrated the compatibility of Swift's network with various blockchain systems.
Chainlink earns fees across every blockchain it serves while Ethereum competes with rival ledgers for deposits, giving LINK a broader monetization edge.
For Chainlink, the key challenge will be turning Swift's ongoing projects into formal, paying contracts and pushing past its recent intraday peak of around $14, about 12% above its current price.
If ETH falls below its September 16 closing price of $2,417, about 9% lower, it could further weaken its position in this comparison.
Ethereum serves as a settlement layer, acting as the shared ledger where tokenized assets, like bonds and funds, are recorded, and ownership is transferred.
Currently, tokenized assets on public blockchains (excluding stablecoins) are valued at roughly $31 billion, with Ethereum holding more than half of that value, far surpassing any other blockchain.
The collaboration has continued yearly, with Swift conducting tokenized fund trades with UBS Asset Management in 2024 and completing tokenized bond transactions with major banks in January 2026.
In June 2026, more than 50 banks joined Project Pangea to facilitate euro and Korean won stablecoin swaps through Chainlink.

On the other hand, Chainlink operates an oracle network, which brings external data—such as prices and interest rates—into blockchain applications.
Its Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP) is crucial for transferring messages and assets between blockchains that cannot communicate directly.

Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) and Chainlink ( CRYPTO: LINK ) both tap into the growing trend of tokenization—the shift of Treasuries, funds, and bank deposits onto blockchains. However, as we move through 2026, ETH has declined, while LINK has risen 7%. So, when considering Ethereum vs. Chainlink, which cryptocurrency is likely to capture more market share as this trend continues to develop?

Both Ethereum and Chainlink performed well recently, with ETH rising by 11% to reach $2,664 and LINK climbing by 12% to $12. What matters, though, is the broader picture, since both cryptocurrencies offer similar pitches for tokenization until you dig into the details.

Ethereum serves as a settlement layer, acting as the shared ledger where tokenized assets, like bonds and funds, are recorded, and ownership is transferred. Currently, tokenized assets on public blockchains (excluding stablecoins) are valued at roughly $31 billion, with Ethereum holding more than half of that value, far surpassing any other blockchain.

On the other hand, Chainlink operates an oracle network, which brings external data—such as prices and interest rates—into blockchain applications. Its Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP) is crucial for transferring messages and assets between blockchains that cannot communicate directly.

As the demand for tokenization grows, Chainlink’s role expands, particularly as BlackRock’s tokenized money market fund, BUIDL, currently holds about $2.8 billion across eight blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana, and Polygon. Chainlink facilitates interactions between these ledgers , while Ethereum retains the largest volume of assets.

Chainlink’s significant partnerships further underscore its potential. Since 2023, Swift, the network banks rely on for cross-border payments, has been testing connections with Chainlink and several major institutions, including Citi and BNP Paribas. In August 2023, they successfully moved tokenized assets between an Ethereum test network and other blockchains. Tom Zschach, Swift’s chief innovation officer, remarked that these tests demonstrated the compatibility of Swift’s network with various blockchain systems.

The collaboration has continued yearly, with Swift conducting tokenized fund trades with UBS Asset Management in 2024 and completing tokenized bond transactions with major banks in January 2026. In June 2026, more than 50 banks joined Project Pangea to facilitate euro and Korean won stablecoin swaps through Chainlink.

However, despite these promising developments, SWIFT and Chainlink have yet to publish a formal fee structure for their projects, meaning Chainlink hasn’t reaped immediate financial rewards from these tests.

Ethereum’s transaction model differs from Chainlink’s. Every transaction on Ethereum incurs a fee paid in ETH, part of which is burned, reducing ETH supply during high-activity periods. Despite this mechanism, the overall ETH supply has increased by about 1% over the last year, mainly because much of the activity now occurs on layer-2 networks that pay only minimal fees to Ethereum.

Conversely, LINK holders see slower growth. Banks and applications compensate node operators—who run the oracle network—with LINK for data and cross-chain communication. Increased activity from financial institutions drives higher demand for LINK, but that demand comes through contracts and billing rather than immediate supply reductions.

Our assessment leans towards Chainlink as the stronger candidate for growth. Financial institutions and asset issuers are diversifying tokenized assets across multiple blockchains, and Chainlink’s services can generate revenue from each chain, including Ethereum. In contrast, Ethereum must compete with various other ledgers for the same deposits. This is reflected in the market trends, with LINK up 7% for 2026 while ETH has remained in the red.

For Chainlink, the key challenge will be turning Swift’s ongoing projects into formal, paying contracts and pushing past its recent intraday peak of around $14, about 12% above its current price. Meanwhile, Ethereum may need to break above its September 21 intraday mark of $2,807, about 5% higher than its recent trading position, to shift market sentiment. If ETH falls below its September 16 closing price of $2,417 , about 9% lower, it could further weaken its position in this comparison.

Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) and Chainlink ( CRYPTO: LINK ) both tap into the growing trend of tokenization—the shift of Treasuries, funds, and bank deposits onto blockchains. However, as we move through 2026, ETH has declined, while LINK has risen 7%. So, when considering Ethereum vs. Chainlink, which cryptocurrency is likely to capture more market share as this trend continues to develop?

Both Ethereum and Chainlink performed well recently, with ETH rising by 11% to reach $2,664 and LINK climbing by 12% to $12. What matters, though, is the broader picture, since both cryptocurrencies offer similar pitches for tokenization until you dig into the details.

Ethereum serves as a settlement layer, acting as the shared ledger where tokenized assets, like bonds and funds, are recorded, and ownership is transferred. Currently, tokenized assets on public blockchains (excluding stablecoins) are valued at roughly $31 billion, with Ethereum holding more than half of that value, far surpassing any other blockchain.

On the other hand, Chainlink operates an oracle network, which brings external data—such as prices and interest rates—into blockchain applications. Its Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP) is crucial for transferring messages and assets between blockchains that cannot communicate directly.

As the demand for tokenization grows, Chainlink’s role expands, particularly as BlackRock’s tokenized money market fund, BUIDL, currently holds about $2.8 billion across eight blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana, and Polygon. Chainlink facilitates interactions between these ledgers , while Ethereum retains the largest volume of assets.

Chainlink’s significant partnerships further underscore its potential. Since 2023, Swift, the network banks rely on for cross-border payments, has been testing connections with Chainlink and several major institutions, including Citi and BNP Paribas. In August 2023, they successfully moved tokenized assets between an Ethereum test network and other blockchains. Tom Zschach, Swift’s chief innovation officer, remarked that these tests demonstrated the compatibility of Swift’s network with various blockchain systems.

The collaboration has continued yearly, with Swift conducting tokenized fund trades with UBS Asset Management in 2024 and completing tokenized bond transactions with major banks in January 2026. In June 2026, more than 50 banks joined Project Pangea to facilitate euro and Korean won stablecoin swaps through Chainlink.

However, despite these promising developments, SWIFT and Chainlink have yet to publish a formal fee structure for their projects, meaning Chainlink hasn’t reaped immediate financial rewards from these tests.

Ethereum’s transaction model differs from Chainlink’s. Every transaction on Ethereum incurs a fee paid in ETH, part of which is burned, reducing ETH supply during high-activity periods. Despite this mechanism, the overall ETH supply has increased by about 1% over the last year, mainly because much of the activity now occurs on layer-2 networks that pay only minimal fees to Ethereum.

Conversely, LINK holders see slower growth. Banks and applications compensate node operators—who run the oracle network—with LINK for data and cross-chain communication. Increased activity from financial institutions drives higher demand for LINK, but that demand comes through contracts and billing rather than immediate supply reductions.

Our assessment leans towards Chainlink as the stronger candidate for growth. Financial institutions and asset issuers are diversifying tokenized assets across multiple blockchains, and Chainlink’s services can generate revenue from each chain, including Ethereum. In contrast, Ethereum must compete with various other ledgers for the same deposits. This is reflected in the market trends, with LINK up 7% for 2026 while ETH has remained in the red.

For Chainlink, the key challenge will be turning Swift’s ongoing projects into formal, paying contracts and pushing past its recent intraday peak of around $14, about 12% above its current price. Meanwhile, Ethereum may need to break above its September 21 intraday mark of $2,807, about 5% higher than its recent trading position, to shift market sentiment. If ETH falls below its September 16 closing price of $2,417 , about 9% lower, it could further weaken its position in this comparison.

The stakes are high, as the difference between a flat year and a negative one is only a daily close above $87,498.
If the price drops below its September 18 close of $80,875, it could trigger a return to the lows seen earlier in September.
Should fund inflows maintain their recent pace, Bitcoin may just manage to finish the year in the green.
If they fade and $80,875 breaks, 2026 goes in the books red.

Those who purchased Bitcoin near last year’s peak are still facing significant losses.
Projections suggest more rate hikes are likely before the end of the year, with the next decision coming on October 28, which falls within the critical trading window for Bitcoin.
Bitcoin sits just a whisker away from erasing its 2026 losses, but a rising rate environment, a stalled Senate bill, and fading short-squeeze fuel threaten to pull it back before December 31 arrives.
Bitcoin and XRP are both clawing back losses in 2026, but one faces a much steeper climb and depends on a single Senate vote to close the gap.
On September 21, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw a remarkable inflow of $999 million, marking the strongest daily total in nearly a year.
Bitcoin just cleared $80,000 for two straight days, but sellers have crushed every rally attempt near $83,000 since late August.
On that same day, spot Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) funds also attracted about $270 million, contributing to the overall crypto market crossing $3 trillion.
Meanwhile, over $800 million in short positions were liquidated within 24 hours, as traders were forced to buy back to cover losses.
